The squared denominator keeps f''s sign equal to the sign of 6x: falling for x < 0, rising for x > 0, within each domain piece. The single critical point is x = 0 with f(0) = (-4)/(-1) = 4 — and since the middle branch dives toward −∞ on both sides as x → ±1, the point (0, 4) is that branch's local maximum. Cross-checking each critical value against its corridor catches errors the algebra alone misses.

Slant asymptotes (degree gap one) integrate the same way: divide, sketch the line, and let the remainder term's sign show which side the curve hugs at each end. BC exams enjoy one rational-function analysis with a slant; the division is Unit 1.7's, the derivative work is this unit's.

The asymptote-aware protocol ordering matters: limits FIRST, derivatives second. Students who compute f' before mapping the asymptotes routinely classify extremes into corridors the curve never visits. Geography before topography.
key_terms: Regions between asymptotes and zeros where the curve's sign is fixed
Asymptotes and end behavior before derivative refinement
Divide, draw the line, sign the remainder to pick the hugging side
boxes: ap_alert

A critical point's classification must be consistent with its corridor: a 'local max' whose value sits below a corridor's floor signals an algebra error. The two-second value-vs-corridor sanity check is free insurance on rational-function questions.

sections.title: The Matching Game
sections.subtitle: f, f', f'' in any pairing
sections.body:
Graph-matching questions show two or three curves and ask which is f, which f', which f''. The decision rules, in order of power: (1) zeros of one curve must align with extremes of another (f' = 0 under f's peaks); (2) where one curve is positive, its antiderivative-partner must rise; (3) inflections of f align with extremes of f' and zeros of f''. Apply rule 1 to candidate pairs and most matchings collapse immediately.

Degree logic shortcuts polynomial matchings: differentiation drops degree by one, so the wiggliest curve (most turning points) is f, the next f', the flattest f''. A cubic-parabola-line trio matches by shape class alone. Trig matchings rotate phases: sine's derivative leads by a quarter period — the curve peaking where another crosses zero RISING is the derivative of the crosser.

The verification habit that prevents traps: after matching, spot-check ONE feature in each direction — 'f has a max at x = 2; does my f' cross zero downward there? f' has a min at 4; does my f'' cross zero upward there?' Thirty seconds, two checks, and the matching is bulletproof. Traps in these questions are mirror-images and sign-flips that survive sloppy matching but die under spot-checks.

Table-direction translations run the same correspondences without pictures: given a table of signs for f, f', f'' on intervals, select the consistent graph (or vice versa). The dashboard from last chapter IS the table; the protocol from this chapter IS the graph. The two formats are one analysis wearing different output devices.
key_terms: Zeros of f' under extremes of f; zeros of f'' under inflections of f
Most wiggles = f; each differentiation smooths one wiggle away
Verify one feature per pairing after matching — kills mirror traps
boxes: ap_alert

In matching questions, test EXTREME-to-ZERO alignment first — it eliminates wrong candidates fastest. Slope-reading ('this curve is positive so that one should rise') is the backup check, not the primary tool; it is slower and easier to fumble under pressure.

sections.title: Consistency Diagnosis
sections.subtitle: When data and graphs disagree
sections.body:
The inverse skill: given a proposed graph plus derivative data, find the inconsistency. 'The table says f'(3) = 0 and f''(3) > 0, but the graph shows a maximum at x = 3' — the 2DT demands a minimum; the graph is wrong. Diagnosis questions reward knowing the implications as two-way streets you can drive in REVERSE: every test that classifies also constrains.

The constraint catalog, assembled from the unit: extremes need f' sign changes (or endpoint status); maxima sit capped, minima cupped (when f'' exists and is nonzero); inflections need f'' sign changes; increasing intervals forbid downhill arcs; concave-up intervals demand the curve sit above its tangent lines. A proposed sketch violating any one is diagnosably wrong, and naming WHICH constraint broke is the answer.

MVT supplies the subtlest diagnostics: a table with f(1) = 3 and f(4) = 3 plus the claim 'f' > 0 on (1, 4)' is self-contradictory — Rolle forces a zero of f' between equal values. Average-rate bounds (MVT) catch impossible tables: f(0) = 0, f(2) = 10 with 'f'(x) ≤ 3 throughout' cannot coexist, since the average rate 5 must be attained. Theorems as lie detectors — the AP's most elegant question genre.

The unit closes where it opened: existence theorems (EVT, Rolle, MVT) plus classification machinery (1DT, 2DT, concavity) form one deductive system. Curve sketching exercises the system forward; consistency diagnosis exercises it backward; the exam exercises it in both directions, often in the same problem. Master the implications, not the rituals.
key_terms: Each test, read backward, forbids graph features — the diagnosis toolkit
Rolle/MVT expose impossible tables: equal values force zero rates; averages must be attained
Forward analysis and backward diagnosis are the same implications, both tested
boxes: ap_alert

'Which of the following could be the graph of f?' questions are elimination races: check each option against ONE strong constraint (usually extreme placement or concavity at a labeled point) and discard fast. Verifying the survivor fully beats verifying all options partially.

mcq.question: f'(x) > 0 and f''(x) < 0 on (2, 5). The graph of f on that interval is
mcq.explanation: Positive slope, negative bend: climbing but flattening — rising, capped.

mcq.question: f(x) = (x² - 4)/(x² - 1) has vertical asymptotes at
mcq.explanation: The denominator x² - 1 vanishes at ±1 with no cancellation (zeros are at ±2). y = 1 is the horizontal asymptote — a different feature.

mcq.question: Three graphs show a cubic, a parabola, and a line. If they are f, f', f'' in some order, then

choices.A: cubic = f, parabola = f', line = f''
choices.B: parabola = f, cubic = f', line = f''
choices.C: line = f, parabola = f', cubic = f''
choices.D: cubic = f, line = f', parabola = f''

mcq.explanation: Differentiation lowers polynomial degree by one: 3 → 2 → 1. Degree logic settles it without reading a single feature.

mcq.question: A table claims f(2) = 7, f(6) = 7, and f'(x) > 0 for all x in (2, 6). This data is

choices.A: impossible — Rolle's Theorem forces f'(c) = 0 somewhere in (2, 6)
choices.B: possible if f is concave up
choices.C: possible if f has an asymptote

mcq.explanation: Equal values at the ends of an interval where f is differentiable force a zero derivative between (Rolle) — 'always positive' contradicts it. (Implicitly f is differentiable since f' is discussed throughout.)

mcq.question: The graph of f'' is positive on (0, 3) and negative on (3, 7). Which feature does the graph of f have at x = 3?
mcq.explanation: f'' changes sign at 3: concavity flips, the definition of an inflection point. (Extremes of f need f' information, which is not given.)

frq.question:
Let f(x) = x³ - 3x² + 4.
(a) Find the intervals of increase/decrease and classify all extremes.
(b) Find the inflection point and the concavity intervals.
(c) Sketch-describe the curve: list the anchor points in order of x and name the arc type (rising/falling, cupped/capped) connecting each consecutive pair. Include end behavior.
rubric: (a) f' = 3x(x - 2): increasing on (-∞,0) and (2,∞), decreasing on (0,2); max at (0,4), min at (2,0)
(b) f'' = 6x - 6: inflection at (1, 2); concave down x < 1, up x > 1
(c) Anchors (0,4), (1,2), (2,0); arcs: rising-capped into (0,4), falling-capped to (1,2), falling-cupped to (2,0), rising-cupped away
End behavior: f → -∞ as x → -∞, f → ∞ as x → ∞
frq.model_answer: (a) f'(x) = 3x² - 6x = 3x(x - 2): positive, negative, positive across 0 and 2. Increasing on (-∞, 0) and (2, ∞); decreasing on (0, 2). Local max at (0, 4) (+ to −); local min at (2, 0) (− to +). (b) f''(x) = 6x - 6: negative before 1, positive after — inflection at (1, f(1)) = (1, 2); concave down on (-∞, 1), up on (1, ∞). (c) Coming from -∞ (end behavior of a positive cubic), the curve rises capped into the peak (0, 4); falls capped to the inflection (1, 2); continues falling but now cupped to the valley (2, 0); rises cupped toward +∞. Four arcs, four taxonomy cells, one S-shaped cubic.

frq.question:
Consider g(x) = x/(x² + 1).
(a) Explain why g has no vertical asymptotes, and find its horizontal asymptote(s).
(b) Find and classify all critical points.
(c) g has three inflection points. Find their x-coordinates. (g''(x) = 2x(x² - 3)/(x² + 1)³.)
rubric: (a) x² + 1 never zero: no VAs; degree rule: y = 0 both directions
(b) g' = (1 - x²)/(x² + 1)²: critical at ±1; min at (-1, -1/2), max at (1, 1/2)
(c) g'' zero at x = 0, ±√3, with sign changes at all three
Inflections at x = -√3, 0, √3
frq.model_answer: (a) The denominator x² + 1 ≥ 1 never vanishes, so no vertical asymptotes. Degrees: 1 below 2, so y = 0 is the horizontal asymptote in both directions. (b) g'(x) = ((x² + 1) - x(2x))/(x² + 1)² = (1 - x²)/(x² + 1)². Critical points x = ±1. Sign of g' is the sign of 1 - x²: negative, positive, negative — local min at (-1, -1/2), local max at (1, 1/2). (c) g''(x) = 2x(x² - 3)/(x² + 1)³ vanishes at x = 0, ±√3. The numerator 2x(x - √3)(x + √3) changes sign at each root (all simple), so all three are inflection points: x = -√3, 0, √3. The odd little curve rises from the axis, dips to -1/2, swings through the origin to +1/2, and settles back to the axis — with the bend flipping three times en route.

frq.question:
A student proposes a graph of a differentiable function h with these features: a local maximum at (2, 5); h decreasing on (2, 6); a local minimum at (6, 1); h concave down on the ENTIRE interval (0, 8).
(a) Use the unit's machinery to find the inconsistency in this proposal.
(b) State the theorem or test that exposes it.
(c) Repair the proposal minimally: change one feature so the description becomes consistent, and justify.
rubric: (a) A local min at 6 needs h' changing − to + (h rising just after 6), and a min sits cupped: h'' ≥ 0 nearby — contradicting concave down throughout
(b) The 2DT/concavity constraint (minima are cupped), or: between a max and a min, h' goes 0 → negative → 0, forcing h' to have a min, i.e., an inflection of h
(c) Repair: allow an inflection in (2, 6) — e.g., concave down on (0, 4), concave up on (4, 8)
Justification: the new concavity permits the cupped minimum at 6
frq.model_answer: (a) The proposal puts a local minimum at (6, 1) inside a region declared concave down. A minimum of a differentiable function is locally CUPPED: just after 6 the curve rises, and rising out of a valley requires the slope to increase through zero — h'' ≥ 0 near 6. Concave down on all of (0, 8) forbids exactly that. (b) The concavity constraint behind the Second Derivative Test exposes it (equivalently: h' falls from 0 at the max to 0 at the min, so h' must bottom out between — an inflection of h, impossible under single-signed h''). (c) Minimal repair: insert an inflection point — say h concave down on (0, 4) and concave up on (4, 8). Then the max at 2 sits capped (consistent), the curve un-bends at 4, and the min at 6 sits cupped (consistent). All other features survive untouched.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: What dimensions make the cheapest can, the largest pasture, the shortest cable? Optimization is calculus earning its keep in the real world — and on the AP, it's a word problem with a five-step skeleton that never changes.
learning_objectives: Translate verbal optimization problems into a function of one variable
Use constraint equations to eliminate variables before differentiating
Find and verify optima with the candidates test or derivative tests
Justify that a critical point is the requested extreme — the graded step
Solve the AP's classic scenarios: fencing, boxes, cans, distances, and costs

sections.title: The Optimization Skeleton
sections.subtitle: Objective, constraint, eliminate, optimize, verify
sections.body:
Every optimization problem runs one skeleton: (1) NAME the quantity to optimize and write its formula — the objective; (2) write the CONSTRAINT equation binding the variables; (3) ELIMINATE variables using the constraint until the objective has one variable, and state that variable's domain; (4) OPTIMIZE: find critical points of the single-variable objective; (5) VERIFY the candidate is the requested max/min and ANSWER the actual question asked.

The pasture classic: maximize the area of a rectangular field with 400 m of fence, one side along a river (unfenced). Objective: A = xy. Constraint: x + 2y = 400 (one x-side plus two y-sides). Eliminate: x = 400 - 2y, so A(y) = (400 - 2y)y = 400y - 2y², with domain 0 < y < 200. Optimize: A' = 400 - 4y = 0 at y = 100. Verify: A'' = -4 < 0 — a max. Answer: y = 100, x = 200, area 20,000 m².

Step 3's domain matters more than students expect: endpoints encode degenerate cases (zero-width fields), and on closed domains the candidates test needs them. When the domain is open, the verification step must argue the interior critical point wins — usually via the 2DT or the 1DT sign pattern.

Step 5's two halves both carry credit: the verification sentence (next section's subject) and answering the QUESTION ASKED — if the problem wants the minimum COST, report dollars, not the dimensions that achieve it. Re-read the question's last sentence before writing the final answer; optimization problems lose more points to mismatched answers than to wrong calculus.
key_terms: The quantity being maximized/minimized, as a formula
Solve the constraint for one variable, substitute into the objective
The eliminated objective's variable has physical bounds — state them
boxes: ap_alert

Write the objective and constraint as LABELED equations before any algebra: 'Maximize A = xy subject to x + 2y = 400.' The labeling sentence is setup credit on FRQs and the single best defense against optimizing the wrong quantity.

sections.title: The Justification Point
sections.subtitle: Proving your candidate is the winner
sections.body:
Finding the critical point earns partial credit; JUSTIFYING that it is the requested extreme earns the rest. The AP accepts three justification routes, each one sentence. Route A — Second Derivative Test: 'A''(y) = -4 < 0, so y = 100 gives a local maximum; as the only critical point in the domain, it is the absolute maximum.' Route B — First Derivative Test: 'A' > 0 for y < 100 and A' < 0 for y > 100, so A increases then decreases: absolute max at y = 100.' Route C — Candidates test (closed domains): the comparison table itself is the justification.

The 'only critical point' clause in Route A is load-bearing: a local max among several critical points might lose globally; a local max that is the ONLY critical point on an interval where the function is differentiable cannot be beaten (the function would need to come back up through another critical point). Examiners look for the clause; include it whenever it is true.

Route B's strength: it proves GLOBAL optimality directly — increasing-then-decreasing leaves no room for rivals. On open domains where endpoints cannot be checked, Route B (or A-plus-only) is the standard play. Route C is mandatory when endpoints are live candidates: a cost function on 1 ≤ r ≤ 5 might bottom out at r = 5.

Ungraded justifications that FEEL convincing but score zero: 'this is obviously the max,' 'the graph shows it,' plugging in two nearby points ('A(99) and A(101) are smaller'). Nearby-point checks prove local-ness at best; the rubric wants derivative-based reasoning. One sentence, one route, every time.
key_terms: Negative f'' plus 'only critical point in the domain' = absolute max
Increasing-then-decreasing proves the absolute claim directly
Closed domain: the comparison table is the justification
boxes: ap_alert

The justification is a dedicated rubric point on every optimization FRQ — historically the most-dropped point in Unit 5. Pre-write the three sentence templates in your head; on exam day, pick the matching route and transcribe.

sections.title: The Scenario Repertory
sections.subtitle: Boxes, cans, distances, and cost mixes
sections.body:
Open-top box from a sheet: cut squares of side x from the corners of a W×L sheet, fold. V(x) = x(W - 2x)(L - 2x), domain 0 < x < min(W,L)/2. Expand, differentiate, solve the quadratic in the domain. The cubic volume with quadratic derivative is the genre's fingerprint.

The cylindrical can: minimize surface area at fixed volume V₀. Objective S = 2πr² + 2πrh; constraint πr²h = V₀ eliminates h = V₀/(πr²): S(r) = 2πr² + 2V₀/r. S' = 4πr - 2V₀/r² = 0 gives r³ = V₀/(2π) — and substituting back, h = 2r: the optimal can is exactly as tall as it is wide. Real cans deviate for manufacturing reasons, an aside that makes the result memorable.

Closest-point problems: minimize the distance from (3, 0) to the parabola y = x². The move that saves algebra: minimize the SQUARED distance D = (x - 3)² + x⁴ — distance and its square share minimizers (squaring is increasing on nonneds), and the square root's chain rule fee vanishes. D' = 2(x - 3) + 4x³ = 0 — solve (here numerically or by inspection-friendly setups on the exam). Declare the squared-distance substitution; it is expected, not sneaky.

Cost mixtures: cable from an offshore platform to a coastal station — underwater segments cost more per mile than overland. Total cost C(x) = c₁√(x² + d²) + c₂(L - x) over the landing point x. C' = 0 balances the marginal costs; the solution typically satisfies a clean sine/ratio condition. These blend the distance template with economic weighting and are BC's favorite hard optimization.
key_terms: V = x(W-2x)(L-2x): cubic objective, quadratic derivative, bounded domain
Fixed volume, min surface ⟹ h = 2r — height equals diameter
Minimize D² instead of D: same winner, no square-root calculus
boxes: ap_alert

When minimizing any distance, write 'minimizing D² minimizes D since squaring preserves order on positive values' and work with D². The sentence licenses the simplification; the simplification halves the differentiation work.

sections.title: Optimization Judgment
sections.subtitle: Domains, units, and the reasonableness pass
sections.body:
Physical domains police the mathematics. Negative lengths, cut-squares larger than the half-sheet, probabilities beyond 1 — constraint violations masquerade as critical points whenever the algebra produces multiple roots. The domain stated in skeleton step 3 is the filter: discard out-of-domain critical points EXPLICITLY ('x = 7 is rejected since the domain is 0 < x < 4'), because the discard is part of the graded logic.

Units ride through optimization like every applied chapter: a maximized area answers in square meters, a minimized cost in dollars, and mixed-rate problems (cost per underwater mile versus overland) demand consistent units before any equation is written. The exam occasionally plants a feet/inches mismatch in the stem; the setup step is where to catch it.

The reasonableness pass after solving: does the optimal can's h = 2r look like a real can (roughly, yes)? Does the pasture use ALL the fence (it must — leftover fence means a bigger field was available)? Is the maximum-volume box's cut between zero and the half-width? Thirty seconds of plausibility checking catches sign errors, domain slips, and constraint misreads that survive the algebra.

Unit synthesis, closing the analytical arc: critical points (Ch 2) found by derivative rules (Units 2-3), classified by sign tests (Ch 3-4), assembled into portraits (Ch 5), now DEPLOYED on applied objectives. The remaining chapter extends behavior analysis to implicit curves — and then Unit 6 changes the question entirely, from slopes to accumulations.
key_terms: Out-of-domain critical points are discarded by name, as graded logic
Plausibility-check the optimum against the physical story
Optimal solutions use the full budget/fence/material — slack signals errors
boxes: ap_alert

If a quadratic derivative yields two roots, expect exactly one in the physical domain — and SAY why the other is rejected. Silent discards leave graders unsure you saw the issue; explicit discards convert a potential deduction into evidence of command.

mcq.question: A farmer has 240 m of fence for a rectangular pen against a barn (no fence on the barn side). The maximum area is
mcq.explanation: A(y) = (240 - 2y)y maximizes at y = 60, x = 120: area 7200 m².

mcq.question: Two nonnegative numbers sum to 20. The maximum value of their product is
mcq.explanation: P = x(20 - x) peaks at x = 10: P = 100.

mcq.question: To minimize the distance from the point (0, 3) to the curve y = x², the cleanest objective function is
mcq.explanation: Squared distance from (0, 3) to (x, x²): x² + (x² - 3)² — same minimizer as D, no radical. (D matches the wrong anchor point.)

mcq.question: An open-top box is made by cutting x-by-x squares from the corners of a 12-by-12 sheet. The domain of the volume function V(x) = x(12 - 2x)² is
mcq.explanation: The fold needs positive base width: 12 - 2x > 0 gives x < 6, with x > 0 for a positive height.

mcq.question: C(r) = 2πr² + 250/r for r > 0 (a can's cost). C'(r) = 4πr - 250/r². The justification that the critical point gives an absolute minimum is best stated as

choices.A: C'' = 8π + 500/r³ > 0 for all r > 0, and it is the only critical point
choices.B: C(r) is large at the critical point
choices.C: C(1) and C(5) are both bigger
choices.D: the graph looks like a valley

mcq.explanation: Positive second derivative everywhere (the function is convex) plus uniqueness of the critical point — Route A at full strength. B is meaningless; C proves only local comparisons; D is ungraded.

frq.question:
A rectangular poster must contain 600 cm² of printed area, with 5 cm margins top and bottom and 3 cm margins on each side. Let x be the WIDTH of the printed area.
(a) Express the total poster area A as a function of x alone, and state the domain.
(b) Find the dimensions of the printed area that minimize the total poster area.
(c) Justify that your answer gives the absolute minimum.
rubric: (a) Printed height = 600/x; A(x) = (x + 6)(600/x + 10), domain x > 0
(c) A'' = 7200/x³ > 0 for all x > 0 and unique critical point ⟹ absolute min
Final dimensions reported for the PRINTED area as asked
frq.model_answer: (a) The printed area is x wide and 600/x tall. The poster adds 3 cm margins each side and 5 cm top and bottom: A(x) = (x + 6)(600/x + 10) = 600 + 10x + 3600/x + 60 = 660 + 10x + 3600/x, for x > 0. (b) A'(x) = 10 - 3600/x² = 0 gives x² = 360, x = 6√10 ≈ 18.97 cm. Printed height: 600/x = 600/(6√10) = 10√10 ≈ 31.62 cm. The printed area should be 6√10 cm wide by 10√10 cm tall. (c) A''(x) = 7200/x³ > 0 for every x in the domain, so the objective is concave up throughout and x = 6√10, the only critical point, gives the absolute minimum total area.

frq.question:
A 10 dm³ (10,000 cm³) closed cylindrical drum is to be built. The material for the top and bottom costs 0.06 dollars/cm², and the side costs 0.04 dollars/cm².
(a) Write the cost as a function of the radius r alone.
(b) Find the radius minimizing the cost. (Leave the answer in exact cube-root form.)
(c) A consultant claims that at the optimal radius, the side costs exactly twice as much as the top and bottom combined. Verify or refute the claim using your optimal r.
rubric: (c) At the optimum 0.24πr³ = 800, so the ends cost 0.12πr² = 400/r while the side costs 800/r — ratio exactly 2
Concludes the claim is TRUE: side costs twice the ends at the optimum
frq.model_answer: (a) Volume: πr²h = 10000, so h = 10000/(πr²). Ends: 2πr² at 0.06 → 0.12πr². Side: 2πrh at 0.04 → 0.08πr·(10000/(πr²)) = 800/r. C(r) = 0.12πr² + 800/r, r > 0. (b) C'(r) = 0.24πr - 800/r² = 0 ⟹ r³ = 800/(0.24π) = 10000/(3π), so r = (10000/(3π))^{1/3} ≈ 10.2 cm. (C'' = 0.24π + 1600/r³ > 0 and the critical point is unique: absolute minimum.) (c) At the optimum, 0.24πr³ = 800, i.e. 0.12πr² = 400/r. The ends cost 0.12πr² = 400/r and the side costs 800/r — exactly twice. The claim is true: the optimal drum splits its budget 2:1 between side and ends, a fingerprint of the 0.04/0.06 price ratio.

frq.question:
A power station is on the bank of a straight river 300 m wide; a factory is 1000 m downstream on the opposite bank. Cable costs $5 per meter underwater and $3 per meter on land. The cable will run underwater from the station to a point P on the opposite bank x meters downstream, then on land from P to the factory.
(a) Write the total cost as a function of x, with domain.
(b) Find the value of x that minimizes the cost.
(c) Verify the minimum with a derivative test and compute the minimum cost.
rubric: Endpoint check or global argument included (closed domain: compare C(0) = 4500, C(1000) ≈ 5220)
frq.model_answer: (a) The underwater leg spans √(x² + 300²) = √(x² + 90000); the land leg is 1000 - x. C(x) = 5√(x² + 90000) + 3(1000 - x), 0 ≤ x ≤ 1000. (b) C'(x) = 5x/√(x² + 90000) - 3 = 0: 5x = 3√(x² + 90000), 25x² = 9x² + 810000, x² = 50625, x = 225 m. (c) C' < 0 for x < 225 and C' > 0 for x > 225 (the ratio 5x/√(...) increases with x), so C falls then rises: absolute minimum at x = 225, confirmed against the endpoints (C(0) = 5·300 + 3000 = 4500; C(1000) = 5√(1090000) + 0 ≈ 5220). Minimum cost: C(225) = 5√(50625 + 90000) + 3(775) = 5(375) + 2325 = 1875 + 2325 = $4200.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: Circles, ellipses, and folium curves don't pass the vertical line test — but they still have flat tops, steep sides, and bending arcs. This closing chapter points the unit's entire toolkit at curves that aren't functions, exactly the way the BC exam likes to.
learning_objectives: Find horizontal and vertical tangent points on implicit curves systematically
Determine concavity of implicit curves via implicit second derivatives
Classify points on implicit curves using sign analysis adapted to branches
Combine implicit differentiation with the unit's tests in FRQ-style sequences
Handle the dual-condition systems (derivative condition + original equation) cleanly

sections.title: Flat Tops and Steep Sides, Revisited
sections.subtitle: The two-equation systems
sections.body:
Unit 3 located horizontal tangents (numerator of dy/dx zero) and vertical tangents (denominator zero) on implicit curves. This unit's lens upgrades the question from WHERE to WHAT: a horizontal-tangent point on a closed curve is typically its highest or lowest point — a constrained extreme — and the locating system doubles as an optimization tool.

The ellipse x² + xy + y² = 12: dy/dx = -(2x + y)/(x + 2y). Horizontal candidates: y = -2x on the curve: x² - 2x² + 4x² = 12 gives x = ±2 — points (2, -4) and (-2, 4). Vertical candidates: x = -2y similarly gives (4, -2), (-4, 2). The four points frame the tilted ellipse: top at (-2, 4), bottom at (2, -4), rightmost (4, -2), leftmost (-4, 2). 'Find the highest point on the curve' is solved by the horizontal-tangent system — implicit optimization without ever isolating y.

The system discipline from Unit 3 persists: the tangent condition AND the original equation, solved simultaneously; candidates where both numerator and denominator vanish get flagged for special handling, not blind classification.

Why the exam loves this: it braids Unit 3 mechanics with Unit 5 interpretation in one problem — typically (a) find dy/dx, (b) locate the horizontal tangent points, (c) classify or interpret them. Parts (a) and (b) are computation; part (c) is this unit. The braid is the single most predictable BC implicit FRQ.
key_terms: Horizontal-tangent points are the curve's local tops and bottoms
Tangent condition + original curve, solved simultaneously
(a) dy/dx, (b) tangent points, (c) classification — the standard sequence
boxes: ap_alert

After solving the horizontal-tangent system, VERIFY the denominator is nonzero at each solution: a point killing both numerator and denominator is not a horizontal tangent but a singular point needing separate analysis. The one-line check ('at (2, -4), x + 2y = -6 ≠ 0 ✓') is graded.

sections.title: Concavity on Implicit Curves
sections.subtitle: y'' with the original equation recycled
sections.body:
Classifying an implicit curve's flat points needs concavity, and concavity needs the implicit second derivative — the Unit 3 workflow (differentiate y', substitute y', recycle the original equation) now serving the 2DT. The circle's y'' = -25/y³ classified its arcs; general curves run the same play with more algebra.

Efficient classification at a SPECIFIC flat point skips the general y'': differentiate the dy/dx expression (or the once-differentiated equation), then substitute the point's x, y, AND y' = 0 — the zero slope kills entire terms, collapsing the computation. On x² + xy + y² = 12 at (2, -4): differentiate 2x + y + (x + 2y)y' = 0 once more to get 2 + 2y' + (1 + 2y')y' + (x + 2y)y'' = 0. Setting y' = 0 at the flat point wipes out the middle terms: 2 + (x + 2y)y'' = 0, so y'' = -2/(x + 2y) = -2/(-6) = 1/3 > 0 — concave up: (2, -4) is the curve's LOW point. The y' = 0 collapse is the technique's entire speed advantage.

The matching classification at (-2, 4): by the same formula y'' = -2/(x + 2y) = -2/6 = -1/3 < 0 — concave down, the HIGH point. Symmetric curves often yield mirrored verdicts from one computation; noticing the symmetry halves the work and signals understanding in written solutions.

The 2DT's statement adapts verbatim: at a point with dy/dx = 0, positive y'' means a local minimum OF THE BRANCH through that point, negative a local maximum. The branch language matters — implicit curves carry several function-branches, and classification is per-branch. The exam's phrasing ('the curve has a local maximum at...') implicitly means the branch, and answering in branch terms is always safe.
key_terms: Substituting the flat point's zero slope before solving for y'' kills most terms
Implicit verdicts are per-branch: the arc through the point cups or caps
Symmetric curves yield mirrored classifications from one computation
boxes: ap_alert

At a horizontal-tangent point, differentiate the ONCE-differentiated equation and immediately set y' = 0 — never compute the general y'' formula first. The collapse turns a quotient-rule marathon into three lines, and BC FRQ rubrics are written expecting the short route.

sections.title: Full Behavior Analysis
sections.subtitle: A worked implicit dossier
sections.body:
The folium-style curve x³ + y³ = 6xy rewards a complete dossier. dy/dx = (2y - x²)/(y² - 2x) (Unit 3 computation). Horizontal tangents: x² = 2y on the curve. Substituting y = x²/2: x³ + x⁶/8 = 3x³, so x⁶ = 16x³ and x³ = 16, giving x = 2^{4/3} and y = x²/2 = 2^{8/3}/2 = 2^{5/3}. The arithmetic is heavier than the concept: one genuine flat point on the loop, at (2^{4/3}, 2^{5/3}). Vertical tangents mirror by the curve's x↔y symmetry: (2^{5/3}, 2^{4/3}).

The symmetry observation does real work: the folium is symmetric across y = x (swap x and y and the equation is unchanged), so every feature reflects — flat points pair with steep points, and one dossier entry generates its mirror for free. Exam curves are chosen with such symmetries; spotting them is both a checker and a shortcut.

Singular points — where numerator AND denominator of dy/dx vanish — get the flagged treatment: for the folium, (0, 0) kills both 2y - x² and y² - 2x. The origin is where the loop crosses itself: two branches, two tangent directions, no single slope. The AP handles singular points gently (usually 'explain why dy/dx is not defined'), and the honest answer names the 0/0 form and the geometric crossing.

The dossier's exam format: a sequence of parts walking exactly this analysis — derivative, tangent points, a classification, sometimes a singular-point comment. Each part feeds the next; an early algebra slip cascades. The defensive practice: carry EXACT values (2^{4/3}, not 2.52) so later parts substitute cleanly, and re-verify each located point ON the original curve before moving on.
key_terms: Derivative, flat/steep points, concavity verdicts, singularities — the complete file
Swap-invariant equations mirror every feature across y = x
Both parts of dy/dx vanish: branches cross, no single tangent exists
boxes: ap_alert

Re-verify located points against the ORIGINAL equation before classifying them — a candidate that fails the curve equation is an algebra-slip artifact, and classifying a phantom point compounds one error into three. The verification line is cheap; the cascade is not.

sections.title: The Unit in One Problem
sections.subtitle: Synthesis and the road to integration
sections.body:
A capstone composite, sketched: the curve x² - xy + y² = 9 (a tilted ellipse). (a) dy/dx = (y - 2x)/(2y - x). (b) Horizontal tangents: y = 2x on the curve gives 3x² = 9, x = ±√3 — points (√3, 2√3) and (-√3, -2√3). (c) Classify: differentiate-and-collapse with y' = 0 gives y'' = -2/(2y - x); at (√3, 2√3): y'' = -2/(3√3) < 0 — the high point. (d) The MVT-flavored finale some FRQs add: between the high and low points, the curve's branches must pass through every intermediate height — IVT on a parametrized arc.

Every move in that composite is a chapter of this unit: critical-point hunting (Ch 2) via implicit systems (Ch 7), classification by the adapted 2DT (Ch 4, 7), existence reasoning (Ch 1). The unit's deliverable is not seven techniques but ONE analytical fluency that reads any curve — explicit, implicit, or data-described — for its behavior.

What the toolkit cannot yet do: measure. How LONG is the arc between the flat points? How much AREA does the closed curve enclose? Slopes and shapes answer 'what does it look like'; the next unit's integral answers 'how much.' The derivative tells the curve's story pointwise; the integral adds it up.

Unit 6 opens with exactly that turn: accumulation, the definite integral, and the theorem — fundamental in name and in fact — that welds the two halves of calculus together. The analytical machinery built here stays loaded: optimization returns inside integral applications, concavity returns in error analysis, and the MVT returns wearing an integral costume. Nothing in this unit retires.
key_terms: One implicit curve exercising the unit's full toolkit in sequence
The unified skill: read behavior from derivatives in any presentation
From slope-questions to amount-questions — Unit 6's integral
boxes: ap_alert

BC implicit FRQs cascade: part (c) uses part (b)'s points and part (a)'s derivative. Budget time to VERIFY parts (a) and (b) before classifying in (c) — thirty seconds of checking beats propagating one slip through three scored parts.

mcq.question: For the curve x² + 4y² = 16, the points with horizontal tangent lines are
mcq.explanation: dy/dx = -x/(4y) = 0 at x = 0; the curve gives 4y² = 16, y = ±2.

mcq.question: On the curve x² + y² = 25, y'' = -25/y³. The arc through (0, -5) is

choices.A: concave up — the point is the circle's bottom
choices.B: concave down — the point is the circle's top

mcq.explanation: y'' = -25/(-125) = 1/5 > 0: cupped. The lowest point of the circle, consistent with dy/dx = 0 there.

mcq.question: For an implicit curve, dy/dx = (3y - x)/(y - 3x). A point where BOTH 3y - x = 0 and y - 3x = 0 hold is

choices.A: a singular point requiring separate analysis

mcq.explanation: 0/0 in the slope formula means no single tangent direction — typically a self-crossing. Neither tangent classification applies without deeper analysis.

mcq.question: At a point on an implicit curve where dy/dx = 0 and (by the collapse computation) y'' = -4/3, the branch through the point has
mcq.explanation: Flat tangent plus negative second derivative: capped — a local max of that branch, by the 2DT.

mcq.question: The curve x³ + y³ = 6xy is unchanged when x and y are swapped. If it has a horizontal tangent at (a, b), it must have
mcq.explanation: Reflection across y = x swaps the roles of horizontal and vertical: the mirrored point carries the mirrored (vertical) tangent.

frq.question:
Consider the curve x² + xy + y² = 12.
(a) Find dy/dx.
(b) Find all points where the curve has a horizontal tangent line, verifying the denominator condition.
(c) Using the collapse technique (substituting y' = 0 after differentiating again), classify each point from (b) as the branch's local maximum or minimum.
rubric: (b) y = -2x into the curve: 3x² = 12, x = ±2 → (2, -4), (-2, 4); checks x + 2y ≠ 0 at both
(c) Differentiating again with y' = 0: 2 + (x + 2y)y'' = 0 → y'' = -2/(x + 2y)
At (2,-4): y'' = 1/3 > 0 local min; at (-2,4): y'' = -1/3 < 0 local max
frq.model_answer: (a) Differentiating: 2x + y + x y' + 2y y' = 0, so dy/dx = -(2x + y)/(x + 2y). (b) Horizontal tangents need 2x + y = 0, i.e., y = -2x, on the curve: x² + x(-2x) + 4x² = 3x² = 12, x = ±2. Points: (2, -4) and (-2, 4). Denominator check: x + 2y = 2 - 8 = -6 ≠ 0 and -2 + 8 = 6 ≠ 0 ✓ — both are genuine horizontal tangents. (c) Differentiate 2x + y + (x + 2y)y' = 0 once more and set y' = 0 at the points: 2 + (x + 2y)y'' = 0, so y'' = -2/(x + 2y). At (2, -4): y'' = -2/(-6) = 1/3 > 0 — the branch cups: local minimum (the curve's lowest point). At (-2, 4): y'' = -2/6 = -1/3 < 0 — local maximum (the highest point).

frq.question:
The curve y³ - xy = 6 passes through (1, 2).
(a) Verify the point and find dy/dx at (1, 2).
(b) Determine whether the curve has any horizontal tangent points at all, and justify.
(c) Find the points where the curve has a VERTICAL tangent line. (The system is 3y² = x with the original equation.)
rubric: (a) 8 - 2 = 6 ✓; differentiating: 3y²y' - y - xy' = 0 → y' = y/(3y² - x); at (1,2): 2/11
(b) Horizontal needs y = 0; substituting y = 0 into the curve gives 0 = 6, impossible — no horizontal tangents
(c) 3y² = x into the curve: y³ - 3y³ = 6 → y³ = -3, y = -3^{1/3}, x = 3·3^{2/3}
Verifies numerator y ≠ 0 at the point — genuine vertical tangent
frq.model_answer: (a) Check: 2³ - (1)(2) = 8 - 2 = 6 ✓. Differentiate: 3y² y' - (y + x y') = 0, so y'(3y² - x) = y and dy/dx = y/(3y² - x). At (1, 2): dy/dx = 2/(12 - 1) = 2/11. (b) A horizontal tangent requires the numerator y = 0. But y = 0 in the curve equation gives 0 - 0 = 6 — impossible. The curve never crosses y = 0, and it has NO horizontal tangent points. (c) Vertical tangents: denominator zero, 3y² = x, substituted into the curve: y³ - (3y²)y = -2y³ = 6, so y³ = -3, y = -3^{1/3} ≈ -1.442, and x = 3y² = 3·3^{2/3} ≈ 6.24. At this point the numerator y ≠ 0, so the tangent is genuinely vertical: the point is (3·3^{2/3}, -3^{1/3}).

frq.question:
An elliptical track is modeled by 4x² + y² = 100 (units in meters).
(a) Find the coordinates of the track's northernmost point using calculus (not inspection), showing the horizontal-tangent system.
(b) Classify the point with an implicit second-derivative computation.
(c) A drone must hover over the track point with the steepest slope dy/dx in magnitude. Explain — using the vertical-tangent analysis — why no such 'steepest finite slope' point exists, and describe what happens to slopes near the track's east and west extremes.
rubric: (a) dy/dx = -4x/y = 0 → x = 0; curve: y² = 100 → northernmost (0, 10)
(b) Differentiate 8x + 2y y' = 0 again, set y' = 0: 8 + 2y y'' = 0 → y'' = -4/y = -2/5 < 0: local max ✓
(c) Slopes -4x/y blow up as y → 0 (points (±5, 0)); for any finite bound there are nearer points with larger slope
Describes |dy/dx| → ∞ approaching the east/west extremes — vertical tangents there
frq.model_answer: (a) Differentiating: 8x + 2y y' = 0, so dy/dx = -4x/y. Horizontal tangent: -4x = 0, x = 0; on the curve y² = 100, y = ±10. The northernmost point is (0, 10). (b) Differentiate 8x + 2y y' = 0 again: 8 + 2(y')² + 2y y'' = 0; at (0, 10) with y' = 0: 8 + 20 y'' = 0, y'' = -2/5 < 0 — concave down: a local maximum of the branch, confirming (0, 10) is the top. (c) The slope -4x/y grows without bound in magnitude as y → 0 along the curve — i.e., approaching the east and west extremes (±5, 0), where the tangents are vertical (denominator zero, numerator -4(±5) ≠ 0). For any candidate 'steepest finite slope' point, track points closer to (±5, 0) have steeper slopes still, so no maximum finite slope exists; the slopes increase without limit toward the vertical-tangent points.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: If water flows in at a known rate for six hours, how much water arrived? Multiply rate by time — unless the rate keeps changing. The definite integral is what 'rate times time' becomes when the rate refuses to hold still, and it is the second pillar of calculus.
learning_objectives: Interpret the definite integral as accumulated change from a rate function
Read definite integrals as signed areas between a curve and the x-axis
Evaluate integrals geometrically using areas of triangles, rectangles, and circles
Apply integral properties: linearity, interval splitting, and reversed bounds
Translate between accumulation language and integral notation in both directions

sections.title: Accumulating a Changing Rate
sections.subtitle: From rate × time to the integral
sections.body:
A constant inflow of 5 L/min for 6 minutes delivers 30 liters: rate times time, the area of a 5-by-6 rectangle on the rate graph. When the rate R(t) varies, no single multiplication works — but slicing time into tiny intervals, multiplying each slice's (nearly constant) rate by its duration, and adding recovers the idea: total ≈ Σ R(tᵢ)Δt. As slices shrink, the sum sharpens into the definite integral ∫₀⁶ R(t) dt — the exact accumulated change.

The notation narrates the construction: the integral sign ∫ is an elongated S for 'sum,' R(t) dt echoes rate-times-tiny-duration, and the bounds 0 and 6 mark the accumulation window. Reading ∫ₐᵇ R(t) dt aloud as 'the total change accumulated from a to b' is the habit that keeps every applied problem honest.

The units multiply accordingly: liters per minute times minutes gives liters — integral units are ALWAYS (integrand units) × (variable units). A rate in cars per hour integrated over hours counts cars; force in newtons integrated over meters yields newton-meters (work). The units check is the fastest sanity test on any applied integral.

The AP's central translation pair, run in both directions: f(b) = f(a) + ∫ₐᵇ f'(t) dt ('final equals initial plus accumulated change') and ∫ₐᵇ f'(t) dt = f(b) - f(a) ('the integral of a rate is the net change'). These sentences anchor Unit 8's applications and appear on virtually every modern FRQ set; learn them as English, not just symbols.
key_terms: ∫ₐᵇ f(t) dt: the limit of rate-times-duration sums — exact accumulated change
Integral units = integrand units × variable units (L/min × min = L)
f(b) = f(a) + ∫ₐᵇ f' dt and its rearrangement — the applied workhorse
boxes: ap_alert

'How much water is in the tank at t = 6?' is f(0) + ∫₀⁶ R(t) dt — initial PLUS accumulation. Forgetting the initial amount is the most common applied-integral error on the exam; the phrase 'plus what was already there' belongs in your setup line.

sections.title: Signed Area
sections.subtitle: What the integral measures on a graph
sections.body:
Geometrically, ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx is the SIGNED area between the curve and the x-axis: regions above the axis count positive, regions below count negative. A rate dipping below zero (water draining, particle moving left) subtracts from the accumulation, and the graph shows the subtraction as below-axis area.

Signed versus total area is the unit's recurring distinction. ∫₀⁴ f dx with f positive on (0, 1) and negative on (1, 4) nets the difference; the TOTAL area enclosed requires ∫|f| — splitting at the zero crossing and flipping the negative piece's sign. The motion translation: integral of velocity is displacement (signed); integral of speed |v| is total distance — Unit 4's distinction, now in integral form.

Geometric evaluation handles the AP's favorite integral format: a piecewise-linear or circular graph of f, with integrals computed from area formulas. Triangles (½bh), rectangles, trapezoids, and — the perennial — semicircles and quarter circles (areas ¼πr², ½πr² read off the figure). Below-axis pieces enter negative: a quarter circle of radius 2 below the axis contributes -π.

The graph-reading protocol: mark the zero crossings, name each region's shape, compute each area, attach signs, add. Five steps, no antiderivatives — and the format appears on every exam because it tests the integral's MEANING rather than its mechanics.
key_terms: Above-axis positive, below-axis negative — the integral's geometric content
Total area integrates |f|: split at zeros, flip negative pieces
Triangles, trapezoids, circle parts — areas read from the figure, signs attached
boxes: ap_alert

Circle pieces in graph-integrals are radius-traps: a semicircular arc spanning [2, 6] has radius 2 (half the span), not 4. Mark the radius on the figure before computing ¼πr² or ½πr² — the misread radius quadruples the area and the error.

sections.title: The Rules of Accumulation
sections.subtitle: Properties that move integrals around
sections.body:
Linearity: ∫(f + g) = ∫f + ∫g and ∫cf = c∫f — integrals split over sums and release constants, exactly like derivatives and for the same limit-law reasons. Splitting: ∫ₐᵇ + ∫ᵦᶜ = ∫ₐᶜ — accumulation over adjacent windows adds, even when b sits OUTSIDE [a, c] (the algebra self-corrects via signs). Reversal: ∫ᵇₐ = -∫ₐᵇ — swapping bounds flips the sign, because accumulating backward undoes.

Two degenerate facts complete the kit: ∫ₐᵃ f = 0 (no window, no accumulation) and the comparison property — if f ≤ g on [a, b], then ∫ₐᵇ f ≤ ∫ₐᵇ g. It powers quick bounds: since 1 ≤ √(1 + x³) ≤ 1 + x³ on [0, 1], the integral of the middle expression is trapped between 1 and 7/4. Bounding integrands bounds integrals — a BC habit that returns in error analysis.

The properties' exam format is the given-values puzzle: knowing ∫₀⁵ f = 12 and ∫₃⁵ f = 4, find ∫₀³ f (answer: 8, by splitting) or ∫₅⁰ 2f (answer: -24, by reversal and linearity). No functions appear — only the algebra of accumulation. Treat the integrals as numbers with bookkeeping rules and the puzzles are arithmetic.

One caution mirrors the derivative side: integrals do NOT split over products or quotients — ∫fg ≠ (∫f)(∫g). The product's integral machinery (integration by parts) waits in chapter 6; until then, products inside integrals are a stop sign, not an invitation to improvise.
key_terms: Splits over sums, releases constant factors — like differentiation
Adjacent windows add; swapped bounds negate
boxes: ap_alert

Given-values puzzles hide the reversal trick: ∫₇² f dx is the negative of the given ∫₂⁷ f dx. Scan the bounds' ORDER before any arithmetic — the flipped-bounds sign error is silent and costs the whole point.

sections.title: The Accumulation Function
sections.subtitle: Integrals with a variable top
sections.body:
Fix the lower bound and let the upper bound roam: g(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt defines a FUNCTION of x — the accumulation function, measuring how much f-area has piled up from a to x. As x sweeps right, g grows where f is positive (area accruing), falls where f is negative, and pauses where f is zero. The variable t inside is a dummy; x lives only in the bound.

Reading g from a graph of f is a tested skill in its own right: g's value at x is the signed area so far — so g has a maximum where f crosses from + to − (accumulation peaks when the deposits turn to withdrawals), g is increasing where f > 0, and g inflects where f has an extreme. The translation table from Unit 5's graph-of-f' genre applies VERBATIM with f playing the role of g's derivative — which the next chapter's Fundamental Theorem will make official.

Worked reading: f piecewise-linear, positive triangle of area 6 on [0, 3], negative triangle of area 2 on [3, 5]. Then g(0) = 0, g(3) = 6 (the peak), g(5) = 4 — climbing to 6, easing back to 4. Asked for g's maximum on [0, 5]: x = 3, 'because g' = f changes from positive to negative there' — Unit 5's justification grammar, one derivative down.

The accumulation function is the unit's conceptual hinge: it converts integrals from numbers into functions, sets up FTC Part 1 (what is g'?), and models real quantities — total rainfall by day x, cars passed by time x — that FRQs describe in exactly this form. The format rewards students who see 'integral with x on top' and immediately think 'a function whose derivative is the integrand.'
key_terms: g(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt: area-so-far as a function of the sweeping bound
The t inside is internal bookkeeping; the function's variable is the bound x
f acts as g's derivative: f's signs/crossings dictate g's rises/extremes
boxes: ap_alert

For g(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt with f given graphically, every Unit 5 question reappears: g increasing where f > 0, g's max where f crosses downward, g's inflections at f's extremes. One memorized correspondence, an entire FRQ genre unlocked.

mcq.question: Water enters a tank at R(t) = 4 + 2t L/min. The amount added between t = 0 and t = 3 is
mcq.explanation: ∫₀³ (4 + 2t) dt — geometrically a trapezoid with parallel sides 4 and 10 over width 3: ½(4 + 10)(3) = 21.

mcq.question: The graph of f consists of a triangle of area 8 above the axis on [0, 4] and a triangle of area 3 below the axis on [4, 6]. ∫₀⁶ f(x) dx =
mcq.explanation: Signed area: +8 - 3 = 5. (Total area would be 11 — the |f| version.)

mcq.question: Given ∫₁⁸ f dx = 10 and ∫₁⁵ f dx = 7, then ∫₈⁵ f dx =
mcq.explanation: ∫₅⁸ f = 10 - 7 = 3 by splitting; reversing the bounds negates: -3.

mcq.question: g(x) = ∫₀ˣ f(t) dt where f is positive on (0, 2), negative on (2, 7). The maximum of g on [0, 7] occurs at x =
mcq.explanation: g climbs while f > 0 and falls after: the accumulation peaks at the downward crossing x = 2.

mcq.question: The graph of f on [0, 4] is the upper semicircle of radius 2 centered at (2, 0). ∫₀⁴ f(x) dx =
mcq.explanation: Half a circle of radius 2: ½π(2²) = 2π, all above the axis.

frq.question:
The rate at which customers enter a store is modeled by a piecewise-linear function E(t) (customers per hour): E rises linearly from E(0) = 0 to E(2) = 60, stays at 60 until t = 5, then falls linearly to E(8) = 0.
(a) Compute ∫₀⁸ E(t) dt using geometry, and interpret the result with units.
(b) The store opened with 12 customers inside, and customers leave at a constant 40 per hour for the whole period. Write an expression for the number of customers inside at time t = 8 and evaluate it.
(c) At what time t is the number of customers inside greatest? Justify with rates.
rubric: (a) Trapezoid: ½(8 + 3)(60) = 330 customers entered
(c) Inside-count rate is E(t) - 40; greatest when the rate changes + to −
E(t) = 40 falling: t = 6 (on the descent from 60 at t=5 to 0 at t=8, E hits 40 at t = 6); justified as sign change of E - 40
frq.model_answer: (a) The region under E is a trapezoid with parallel sides of lengths 8 (the full base, 0 to 8) and 3 (the top, 2 to 5) and height 60: ∫₀⁸ E dt = ½(8 + 3)(60) = 330. In context: 330 customers entered the store during the 8 hours. (b) Inside at t = 8: initial + entered − left = 12 + 330 - 40(8) = 12 + 330 - 320 = 22 customers. (c) The count inside changes at rate E(t) - 40. E - 40 > 0 once E exceeds 40 (at t = 4/3 on the rise) and stays positive until E falls back to 40: on the descent E(t) = 60 - 20(t - 5), which equals 40 at t = 6. The rate flips from + to − at t = 6, so the store is fullest at t = 6 hours.

frq.question:
The graph of f on [-4, 4] consists of three pieces: a semicircle of radius 1 centered at (-3, 0) lying below the x-axis from (-4, 0) to (-2, 0); a line segment from (-2, 0) to (0, 2); and a line segment from (0, 2) to (4, -2).
(a) Evaluate ∫₋₄⁻² f, ∫₋₂⁰ f, and ∫₀⁴ f.
(b) Evaluate ∫₋₄⁴ f(x) dx.
(c) Find the total area between f and the x-axis on [-4, 4].
rubric: (a) Semicircle below: -π/2; triangle: +2; the [0,4] piece crosses zero at x = 2: +2 then -2, net 0
(c) Total area: π/2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 + π/2
Zero crossing at x = 2 identified and used to split
frq.model_answer: (a) The semicircle of radius 1 below the axis contributes -½π(1²) = -π/2. The triangle from (-2, 0) to (0, 2) has area ½(2)(2) = 2, above the axis: +2. On [0, 4], the line from (0, 2) to (4, -2) crosses zero at x = 2: a positive triangle ½(2)(2) = +2 then a negative one -2: net 0. (b) ∫₋₄⁴ f = -π/2 + 2 + 0 = 2 - π/2. (c) Total (unsigned) area: π/2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 + π/2.

frq.question:
Let g(x) = ∫₂ˣ f(t) dt, where f is graphed: f is positive on (0, 3), zero at 3, negative on (3, 7), with ∫₂³ f = 5 and ∫₃⁷ f = -9.
(a) Compute g(2), g(3), and g(7).
(b) On what interval is g increasing? Justify in terms of f.
(c) Find the minimum value of g on [2, 7], with justification.
rubric: (b) g increasing where f > 0: on (2, 3)
(c) Candidates: endpoints and the sign change; g falls from 5 throughout (3,7)
Minimum g(7) = -4, since g decreases on (3, 7) and ends lowest there
frq.model_answer: (a) g(2) = ∫₂² f = 0. g(3) = ∫₂³ f = 5. g(7) = ∫₂⁷ f = 5 + (-9) = -4. (b) g grows exactly where new area is positive — where f > 0: the interval (2, 3). (c) g rises to 5 at x = 3, then falls steadily across (3, 7) (f < 0 there) to g(7) = -4. The candidates for the minimum are x = 2 (value 0) and x = 7 (value -4): the minimum value is -4 at x = 7, justified because g' = f < 0 on (3, 7) makes g strictly decreasing after its peak, so the right endpoint is lowest.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: Before integrals had antiderivatives, they had rectangles. Riemann sums approximate area with arithmetic anyone can do — and the AP grades the setup, the over/under reasoning, and the trapezoid upgrade every single year.
learning_objectives: Construct left, right, and midpoint Riemann sums from formulas and tables
Compute trapezoidal approximations, including unequal subinterval widths
Determine over/underestimate direction from monotonicity (rectangles) and concavity (trapezoids)
Express a definite integral as a limit of Riemann sums and vice versa
Choose sample points and widths correctly from table data on the exam's terms

sections.title: Rectangles Under a Curve
sections.subtitle: Left, right, and midpoint sums
sections.body:
Slice [a, b] into n subintervals of width Δx = (b - a)/n and erect a rectangle on each, with height read from f at a chosen sample point: the LEFT endpoint (left Riemann sum), RIGHT endpoint (right sum), or MIDPOINT (midpoint sum). Each rectangle contributes height × width; the sum approximates ∫ₐᵇ f dx, with the choice of sample point setting the bias.

Worked on f(x) = x² over [0, 2] with n = 4 (Δx = ½): left sum uses heights at 0, ½, 1, 3/2: (0 + ¼ + 1 + 9/4)(½) = 7/4 = 1.75. Right sum uses ½, 1, 3/2, 2: (¼ + 1 + 9/4 + 4)(½) = 15/4 = 3.75. The true value (next chapters) is 8/3 ≈ 2.67 — bracketed by the two, as an increasing function guarantees. Midpoint, using ¼, ¾, 5/4, 7/4: (1/16 + 9/16 + 25/16 + 49/16)(½) = 84/32 = 2.625 — strikingly closer, a pattern that is no accident.

From tables — the AP's preferred delivery — the subintervals come pre-cut by the data, often with UNEQUAL widths: t-values 0, 2, 5, 6 give widths 2, 3, 1, and each rectangle's width must be read individually. The left sum uses each subinterval's left-edge value; no Δx formula applies. Unequal widths are the norm on FRQs, and hard-coding (b-a)/n is the trap.

Indexing discipline prevents the classic off-by-one: with n subintervals, a left sum uses values at the first n points (skipping the last), a right sum the last n (skipping the first). Writing the sample values in a row and bracketing which n get used beats any formula memorized blind.
key_terms: Σ f(sample)·width over the subintervals — rectangle areas standing in for the integral
Left, right, or midpoint of each subinterval sets the rectangle heights and the bias
Table data pre-cuts the intervals; each width is read, not computed from (b-a)/n
boxes: ap_alert

Table-based Riemann FRQs grade the SETUP: write the sum as height₁·width₁ + height₂·width₂ + ⋯ with the actual numbers visible. A bare final answer cannot earn the setup point, and with unequal widths the visible setup is also your own error-catcher.

sections.title: Over or Under, Part 1
sections.subtitle: Monotonicity decides for rectangles
sections.body:
For an INCREASING function, every left-endpoint rectangle sits below the curve (the left edge is the interval's lowest point): the left sum UNDERestimates, and symmetrically the right sum OVERestimates. For a DECREASING function, the roles flip: left over, right under. The mnemonic is unnecessary if you sketch one subinterval — but the conclusion sentence is graded, so the reasoning must be stated, not just used.

The graded sentence pattern: 'Since f is increasing on [a, b], the left Riemann sum underestimates ∫ₐᵇ f dx.' Cause (monotonicity), claim (direction). On table problems, monotonicity is read from the data (values steadily rising); on formula problems, from f' > 0. Either certificate works; one must appear.

Non-monotonic intervals void the simple rules: a function rising then falling can make a left sum land on either side. Exam questions either keep f monotone or split the analysis at the turn — and 'no conclusion without monotonicity' is itself a tested answer choice. The honest reflex: check the behavior FIRST, then claim a direction.

Midpoint sums resist monotonicity analysis (the midpoint rectangle overshoots on one half, undershoots on the other) — their bias is governed by CONCAVITY: for concave-up f, midpoint underestimates; concave-down, overestimates. The full midpoint story pairs with trapezoids in the next section, where the two make opposite errors and the geometry explains both at once.
key_terms: Left edges are minima of rising intervals; right edges are maxima
The direction claim must cite monotonicity (or the data trend) explicitly
No simple over/under verdict on intervals where f turns around
boxes: ap_alert

The over/under sentence is its own rubric point and must include the word 'increasing' or 'decreasing' (or the data-trend equivalent). 'Left sums underestimate' as a bare slogan is FALSE for decreasing functions — and the exam rotates both cases deliberately.

sections.title: Trapezoids and the Midpoint Duel
sections.subtitle: Slanted tops, concavity bias
sections.body:
Replace each rectangle's flat top with a slanted segment joining the curve's values at both edges: the trapezoid sum, T = Σ ½(f(left) + f(right))·width. Equivalently, T is the average of the left and right sums when widths are equal. Trapezoids hug curves far better than rectangles — error shrinks like 1/n² versus 1/n — and the AP uses them as the default 'good' approximation on table problems.

Trapezoid bias is pure concavity: on a CONCAVE-DOWN arc, the chord joining two curve points sags below the arc, so the trapezoid UNDERestimates; concave-up, chords sit above arcs — overestimate. (Chords below arcs for caps, above for cups: the tangent-line picture from linearization, mirrored — tangents and chords always bracket the curve from opposite sides.)

The midpoint sum makes exactly the OPPOSITE error: the midpoint rectangle equals (in area) the tangent-line trapezoid at the midpoint, and tangents sit below cups, above caps. So for concave-up f: midpoint under, trapezoid over — and the true integral lies between them, with the midpoint typically about half as wrong. The bracket-by-opposites structure is a BC-flavored insight the exam rewards in 'which is largest?' rankings.

The ranking question, assembled: for f increasing and concave up on [a, b], order L < M < ∫ < T < R. Left/right from monotonicity, mid/trap from concavity. Any specific case can be re-derived in seconds from the two principles — derive, don't memorize, because the exam permutes the function's behavior precisely to break memorized orderings.
key_terms: Σ ½(f(L) + f(R))·width — chord-topped slices, the average of L and R sums
Chords under caps (trap under), over cups (trap over); midpoint mirrors it
Midpoint and trapezoid err oppositely; the integral sits between
boxes: ap_alert

Trapezoid questions on tables with UNEQUAL widths must be computed trapezoid-by-trapezoid: ½(f₀ + f₁)w₁ + ½(f₁ + f₂)w₂ + ⋯. The averaged-sums shortcut T = (L + R)/2 silently assumes equal widths — using it on FRQ tables is a wrong answer, not a shortcut.

sections.title: The Limit Definition
sections.subtitle: Sums become integrals, and back
sections.body:
The definite integral IS the limit: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = lim n→∞ Σᵢ f(xᵢ*)Δx — rectangles refined until the approximation error vanishes. The definition matters operationally on the AP in one specific genre: converting between limit-of-sum notation and integral notation, in both directions.

Reading a limit as an integral: lim n→∞ Σ (3/n)·√(1 + 3i/n) — the factor 3/n is Δx, so the interval has length 3; the sample 1 + 3i/n starts at 1 (right endpoints), so [a, b] = [1, 4] and the integrand is √x: the limit equals ∫₁⁴ √x dx. The decode recipe: identify Δx for the length, the sample expression's range for the bounds, and the function applied to the sample for the integrand.

Writing an integral as a limit reverses the recipe: ∫₂⁵ x³ dx = lim Σ (3/n)(2 + 3i/n)³ with right endpoints. The skeleton — Δx = (b-a)/n, xᵢ = a + iΔx, sum f(xᵢ)Δx — assembles any such expression. Both directions appear as multiple choice; the decode direction is the more common and the more fumbled.

Why the definition earns its keep beyond notation: it is what makes the integral MEAN accumulated change (chapter 1's slicing argument, formalized), it justifies every numerical method in this chapter, and it returns in BC's arc length and surface integrals where slicing arguments construct new integral formulas from scratch. The rectangles never really leave; they just go backstage.
key_terms: ∫ₐᵇ f dx = lim Σ f(xᵢ*)Δx — the integral as refined rectangle sums
Δx gives the length; the sample's range gives the bounds; the applied function is the integrand
The definition's pattern builds new integral formulas (arc length, volumes) later
boxes: ap_alert

In limit-to-integral decodes, the bounds hide in the SAMPLE expression: 2 + 3i/n runs from 2 to 5 as i runs 1 to n — bounds [2, 5], length 3, matching Δx = 3/n. Cross-check length against Δx every time; mismatches expose a misread.

mcq.question: Using the table t: 0, 2, 5, 6 with f(t): 3, 7, 11, 9, the left Riemann sum for ∫₀⁶ f dt is
f is decreasing on [1, 9]. The right Riemann sum for ∫₁⁹ f dx is
mcq.explanation: For decreasing f, each right edge is the interval's lowest point: rectangles sit below the curve.

mcq.question: f is concave down on [0, 8]. The trapezoidal approximation of ∫₀⁸ f dx is
mcq.explanation: Chords sag below concave-down arcs: trapezoid tops sit under the curve. (Monotonicity is irrelevant for trapezoids.)

mcq.question: Using the same table as before (t: 0, 2, 5, 6; f: 3, 7, 11, 9), the trapezoidal approximation of ∫₀⁶ f dt is
lim n→∞ Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ (2/n)·(1 + 2i/n)² equals
mcq.explanation: Δx = 2/n (length 2); samples 1 + 2i/n sweep (1, 3]: bounds [1, 3]; the function applied is squaring. (D is also equivalent by substitution but A is the direct decode; on the exam only one appears.)

frq.question:
A pump's flow rate R(t) (gallons per minute) is recorded: t = 0, 3, 4, 7, 10 with R = 20, 26, 28, 22, 16.
(a) Approximate ∫₀¹⁰ R(t) dt with a right Riemann sum using the four subintervals given, and interpret the result.
(b) Approximate the same integral with a trapezoidal sum.
(c) The pump's rate is known to have been increasing on [0, 4] and decreasing on [4, 10]. Can you determine whether your answer to (a) over- or underestimates on the FULL interval? Analyze each piece.
rubric: (c) On [0,4] (increasing): right sum over; on [4,10] (decreasing): right sum under
Conclusion: opposing biases — no overall verdict without more information
frq.model_answer: (a) Right sum with widths 3, 1, 3, 3 and right heights 26, 28, 22, 16: 26(3) + 28(1) + 22(3) + 16(3) = 220. Approximately 220 gallons flowed through the pump during the 10 minutes. (b) Trapezoids: ½(20+26)(3) + ½(26+28)(1) + ½(28+22)(3) + ½(22+16)(3) = 69 + 27 + 75 + 57 = 228 gallons. (c) On [0, 4], R increases, so right rectangles OVERestimate that portion; on [4, 10], R decreases, so right rectangles UNDERestimate there. The two biases oppose, and without knowing the relative sizes of the errors, no over/under verdict applies to the full-interval estimate — the honest answer is that the direction cannot be determined.

frq.question:
Let f(x) = e^{-x²} on [0, 2], a positive, decreasing, initially concave-down function with an inflection at x = 1/√2.
(a) With n = 4 equal subintervals, write (do not evaluate) the left Riemann sum for ∫₀² f dx.
(b) State whether the left sum over- or underestimates the integral, with justification.
(c) Rank L (left), T (trapezoid), and the true integral I on [0, 1/√2] only — where f is concave down — from smallest to largest, justifying each comparison.
rubric: (b) f decreasing ⟹ left endpoints are maxima ⟹ overestimate
(c) On concave-down: T < I (chords sag); f decreasing: L > I
Ranking: T < I < L
frq.model_answer: (a) Δx = ½: L = ½[e⁰ + e^{-1/4} + e^{-1} + e^{-9/4}]. (b) f is decreasing on [0, 2], so each left endpoint gives the subinterval's largest value — the rectangles poke above the curve: the left sum OVERestimates. (c) On [0, 1/√2], f is concave down: trapezoid chords sag below the arc, so T < I. f is decreasing there, so the left sum overshoots: L > I. Ranking: T < I < L.

frq.question:
Consider lim n→∞ Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ (5/n)·sin(π(2 + 5i/n)).
(a) Identify Δx, the interval [a, b], and the integrand, and rewrite the limit as a definite integral.
(b) A student claims the interval is [0, 5] 'because the sum runs from i = 1 to n.' Explain the error.
(c) Without evaluating, state whether the integral is positive, negative, or requires more analysis, given that sin is being sampled over the resulting interval.
rubric: (a) Δx = 5/n; samples 2 + 5i/n sweep (2, 7]: ∫₂⁷ sin(πx) dx
(b) The index range sets the COUNT of rectangles; the BOUNDS come from the sample expression's sweep, 2 to 7
(c) sin(πx) completes full periods on intervals of length 2; [2, 7] is 2.5 periods
Full periods cancel; the leftover [6, 7] gives ∫ sin(πx) > 0 on (6,7)? sin(πx) on (6,7): πx in (6π,7π), sine positive there — integral positive
frq.model_answer: (a) Δx = 5/n, so the interval has length 5; the sample 2 + 5i/n runs from just above 2 (i = 1) to 7 (i = n): [a, b] = [2, 7], right endpoints. The function applied is sin(π·). The limit equals ∫₂⁷ sin(πx) dx. (b) The summation index i counts the n rectangles — it never names the x-interval. The bounds live inside the sample expression: as i sweeps 1 to n, the sample sweeps 2 to 7. Reading bounds from the index is the standard decode error. (c) sin(πx) has period 2, and [2, 7] spans 2.5 periods. Each complete period integrates to zero, leaving ∫₆⁷ sin(πx) dx; on (6, 7), πx lies in (6π, 7π) where sine is positive. The integral is positive (its value is 2/π, though no evaluation was required).

subject: AP Calculus BC
chapter_title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus — Part 1
hook: Here is the theorem that earns the adjective: the derivative of an accumulation function is the function being accumulated. Slopes and areas — built from opposite ends of calculus — turn out to be inverse operations, and everything after this page depends on it.
learning_objectives: State FTC Part 1: d/dx ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt = f(x) for continuous f
Differentiate accumulation functions, including chain-rule upper bounds
Handle variable lower bounds and two-variable-bound integrals
Analyze accumulation functions (extremes, concavity) using FTC-supplied derivatives
Explain the theorem's meaning: accumulation rate equals the current integrand value

sections.title: The Theorem and Its Meaning
sections.subtitle: Why accumulation differentiates to the integrand
sections.body:
FTC Part 1: if f is continuous on an interval containing a, then g(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt is differentiable and g'(x) = f(x). Differentiating an accumulation function hands back the integrand, evaluated at the sweeping bound. Integration and differentiation are inverse processes — the fact that makes antiderivatives compute areas (Part 2, next chapter) and makes the last chapter's graph-reading correspondences exact.

The intuition deserves to be owned, not memorized: g(x + h) - g(x) is the area of the sliver between x and x + h — a near-rectangle of height f(x) and width h. So the difference quotient (g(x+h) - g(x))/h ≈ f(x)·h/h = f(x), and the limit seals it. The accumulation's growth RATE is the current deposit rate: if water pours at 7 L/min right now, the total's rate of change is 7 L/min right now. Stated that way, the deepest theorem in the course sounds obvious — which is exactly the right way to remember it.

The dummy-variable hygiene from chapter 1 pays off here: in d/dx ∫₂ˣ cos(t²) dt = cos(x²), the t was internal; the answer substitutes the BOUND into the integrand. No antiderivative of cos(t²) exists in elementary terms — and none is needed. FTC1 differentiates integrals you could never evaluate, which is precisely its working power on the exam.

Immediate dividends: every chapter-1 graph correspondence ('g has a max where f crosses + to −') is now literally Unit 5's first-derivative test applied to g' = f. The machinery was never an analogy; it was the theorem, previewed.
key_terms: d/dx ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt = f(x): the accumulation's derivative is the integrand at the bound
g(x+h) - g(x) ≈ f(x)·h: the next sliver of area is a thin rectangle
FTC1 differentiates ∫ cos(t²) dt and friends — no antiderivative required
boxes: ap_alert

d/dx ∫₅ˣ √(1 + t³) dt = √(1 + x³). One substitution, done. Students who try to FIND an antiderivative first are answering a much harder question than was asked — FTC1 problems are recognition problems, not integration problems.

sections.title: Chain Rule Upper Bounds
sections.subtitle: When x² rides on top
sections.body:
When the upper bound is a FUNCTION of x, the accumulation is a composition and the chain rule collects its fee: d/dx ∫ₐ^{u(x)} f(t) dt = f(u(x))·u'(x). Substitute the bound into the integrand, multiply by the bound's derivative. For F(x) = ∫₀^{x²} sin(t) dt: F'(x) = sin(x²)·2x.

The structure is g(u(x)) with g the plain accumulation function: FTC1 gives g' = f, the chain rule glues on u'. Seeing the two-layer anatomy keeps the formula from being one more memorized incantation — it is Unit 3's chain rule meeting this chapter's theorem, nothing new under the hood.

Variable LOWER bounds flip sign first: ∫_{v(x)}^{b} f dt = -∫_b^{v(x)} f dt, so its derivative is -f(v(x))·v'(x). Both bounds variable splits at any convenient constant: d/dx ∫_{v(x)}^{u(x)} f dt = f(u(x))·u'(x) - f(v(x))·v'(x) — 'top in, times top-prime, MINUS bottom in, times bottom-prime.' The two-bound formula compresses the whole section.

Worked at full strength: d/dx ∫_{√x}^{x³} ln(1 + t²) dt = ln(1 + x⁶)·3x² - ln(1 + x)·(1/(2√x)). Mechanical once the anatomy is seen: each bound contributes (integrand at bound)·(bound's derivative), signed by its position. Exam variants stop at one variable bound plus a constant — the full two-bound version is BC-comfortable insurance.
key_terms: d/dx ∫ₐ^{u} f dt = f(u)·u' — substitute the bound, pay its fee
Variable bottoms differentiate with a minus: -f(v)·v'
Top-in times top-prime, minus bottom-in times bottom-prime
boxes: ap_alert

The chain-rule fee on FTC1 problems is the unit's most-planted distractor: d/dx ∫₀^{x²} sin t dt = sin(x²)·2x, and the fee-free sin(x²) sits among the choices every time. Bound a function of x? Fee due. No exceptions.

sections.title: Analyzing Accumulation Functions
sections.subtitle: Unit 5's machinery, fully powered
sections.body:
With g' = f in hand officially, every analytical question about g routes through f. Critical points of g: zeros and sign changes of f. g increasing: f > 0. Concavity of g: monotonicity of f (g'' = f'). Inflections of g: extremes of f. The complete Unit 5 playbook applies with the graph of f as the given — and this composite IS the AP's single most reliable FRQ, appearing in some form nearly every year.

The standard problem hands you a piecewise graph of f (lines and circle arcs) and g(x) = ∫₀ˣ f(t) dt, then walks the ladder: evaluate g at named points (geometric areas with signs), find where g is increasing (f > 0), classify g's critical points (f's crossings, by the 1DT), locate g's inflections (f's extremes), and sketch or bound g. Each rung is a chapter already taught; the FRQ is an assembly test.

Justification grammar carries over verbatim with g' = f cited: 'g has a local maximum at x = 3 because g'(x) = f(x) changes from positive to negative at x = 3.' The phrase g' = f — the theorem's invocation — is part of the graded sentence. Concavity answers cite f's behavior: 'g is concave down on (1, 4) because g' = f is decreasing there.'

Extreme-value versions add the candidates test: absolute extremes of g on [0, 8] compare g's values at endpoints and at f's sign changes, with g-values computed as accumulated areas. The arithmetic is chapter 1; the candidate logic is Unit 5; the bridge is the theorem. Three units in one problem — the reason this FRQ genre decides scores.
key_terms: Evaluate g, analyze g's behavior, classify, sketch — all from f's graph
'g'(x) = f(x)' appears in every justification — the theorem is cited, not assumed
Absolute extremes of g: compare accumulated-area values at crossings and endpoints
boxes: ap_alert

On accumulation FRQs, write 'g'(x) = f(x) by the Fundamental Theorem' once at the top of your work, then reference it. The single line activates Unit 5 grammar for every subsequent part and collects the theorem-citation point examiners look for.

sections.title: Defined by Integrals
sections.subtitle: Functions the integral builds from scratch
sections.body:
Some functions are DEFINED as accumulation integrals because no simpler formula exists. The premier example is the natural logarithm, constructible as ln(x) = ∫₁ˣ (1/t) dt: FTC1 instantly gives d/dx ln x = 1/x, and the log's properties (ln(ab) = ln a + ln b) can be derived from integral algebra. What Unit 2 asserted, the integral constructs.

Statistics runs on another: the error function erf(x) accumulates the bell curve e^{-t²}, which has no elementary antiderivative. Fresnel integrals (sin(t²)) drive optics. These functions are not exotic — they are what accumulation produces when the integrand resists closed forms, and FTC1 supplies their derivatives, their increasing/decreasing analysis, and (in Unit 10) their Taylor series — their entire calculus, formula-free.

For the AP, the operational point: a function presented as g(x) = 3 + ∫₂ˣ f(t) dt is a complete, analyzable object. Its value at 2 is 3 (the integral vanishes); its derivative is f; its tangent line at x = 2 is y = 3 + f(2)(x - 2). Initial value plus accumulated change — the chapter-1 sentence — IS this presentation, and FRQs phrase real models this way constantly.

The theorem's two halves are about to meet: Part 1 says accumulation functions are antiderivatives of their integrands. Part 2 (next chapter) runs the logic backward — ANY antiderivative, however obtained, evaluates the definite integral by subtraction. Together they collapse area computation from rectangle limits to algebra, and the unit's remaining chapters are the craft of finding antiderivatives.
key_terms: ln, erf, Fresnel — built by accumulation when formulas don't exist
g = C + ∫ₐˣ f: value, derivative, tangent, behavior — all readable
Accumulations are antiderivatives; Part 2 turns antiderivatives into evaluations
boxes: ap_alert

g(x) = 5 + ∫₃ˣ f(t) dt has g(3) = 5 — the integral from 3 to 3 is zero, leaving the constant. The 'find g at the anchor point' question is a freebie hidden in nearly every accumulation FRQ; collect it in five seconds.

mcq.question: If g(x) = ∫₁ˣ √(t³ + 1) dt, then g'(2) =

choices.C: Both A and B (they are equal)
choices.D: Cannot be determined without an antiderivative

mcq.explanation: FTC1: g'(x) = √(x³ + 1), so g'(2) = √9 = 3. No antiderivative needed — that is the theorem's point.

mcq.question: d/dx ∫₀^{x³} cos(t) dt =
mcq.explanation: Substitute the bound, multiply by its derivative: cos(x³)·3x². Choice B dodges the chain-rule fee.

mcq.question: F(x) = ∫ₓ⁵ e^{t²} dt. Then F'(x) =
mcq.explanation: The variable bound is on the BOTTOM: flip the integral's sign first, so F' = -e^{x²}.

mcq.question: g(x) = ∫₀ˣ f(t) dt where the graph of f crosses the x-axis from below to above at x = 4. At x = 4, g has
mcq.explanation: g' = f changes − to + at 4: the first derivative test gives a local min of g.

mcq.question: h(x) = 7 + ∫₂ˣ sin(t²) dt. The tangent line to h at x = 2 is
mcq.explanation: h(2) = 7 (empty integral) and h'(2) = sin(4) by FTC1: point-slope assembles A.

frq.question:
The graph of f on [-2, 6] consists of line segments: from (-2, 2) to (0, 2), from (0, 2) to (2, -2), and from (2, -2) to (6, 2) — crossing zero at x = 1 and x = 4. Let g(x) = ∫₀ˣ f(t) dt.
(a) Compute g(-2), g(1), and g(4).
(b) Find the x-coordinates of all local extremes of g on (-2, 6) and classify them, citing the theorem that licenses your reasoning.
(c) On what interval(s) is g concave up? Justify.
rubric: (b) g' = f by FTC1; f: + on (-2,1), − on (1,4), + on (4,6): local max at x = 1, local min at x = 4
(c) g'' = f': f increasing on (2, 6) — g concave up there
Justifications cite g' = f and the sign changes
frq.model_answer: (a) g(1): triangle from 0 to 1 under the descending segment — f falls from 2 at x=0 to 0 at x=1: area ½(1)(2) = 1, so g(1) = 1. g(4) = g(1) + ∫₁⁴ f: the below-axis triangle from 1 to 4 has area ½(3)(2) = 3, so g(4) = 1 - 3 = -2. g(-2) = ∫₀⁻² f = -∫₋₂⁰ f = -(2·2) = -4 (rectangle of height 2, width 2, reversed bounds). (b) By the Fundamental Theorem, g'(x) = f(x). f changes from + to − at x = 1 (local maximum of g) and from − to + at x = 4 (local minimum of g). (c) g''(x) = f'(x): f is increasing on (2, 6) (the rising segment), so g is concave up on (2, 6).

frq.question:
Let F(x) = ∫₁^{x²} (ln t)/t dt for x > 1.
(a) Find F'(x), showing the chain-rule structure, and simplify using ln(x²) = 2 ln x.
(b) Solve F'(x) = 0 on the domain and explain what the result tells you about F.
(c) Compute F''(x) and determine the concavity of F for x > 1.
rubric: (a) F'(x) = (ln(x²)/x²)·2x, then ln(x²) = 2 ln x simplifies it to 4 ln x/x
(b) F' = 4 ln x/x = 0 only at ln x = 0, x = 1 (boundary); F' > 0 for x > 1: F strictly increasing
(c) F'' = 4(1 - ln x)/x²: positive on (1, e), negative on (e, ∞)
Concave up on (1, e), down on (e, ∞), inflection at x = e
frq.model_answer: (a) FTC1 with chain rule, u = x²: F'(x) = (ln(x²)/x²)·2x. Since ln(x²) = 2 ln x, this simplifies to F'(x) = (2 ln x/x²)(2x) = 4 ln x/x. (b) F'(x) = 4 ln x/x = 0 requires ln x = 0, i.e., x = 1 — the domain's edge. For all x > 1, ln x > 0 so F' > 0: F is strictly increasing on its whole domain, with no interior critical points. (c) F''(x) = 4·(x·(1/x) - ln x)/x² = 4(1 - ln x)/x². Positive when ln x < 1 (x < e), negative when x > e: F is concave up on (1, e), concave down on (e, ∞), with an inflection at x = e.

frq.question:
A reservoir's inflow rate is f(t) (acre-feet per day), graphed for 0 ≤ t ≤ 12: f is positive on (0, 5), negative on (5, 9), positive on (9, 12), with ∫₀⁵ f = 40, ∫₅⁹ f = -25, ∫₉¹² f = 10. The reservoir holds A(t) = 100 + ∫₀ᵗ f(s) ds acre-feet.
(a) Compute A(0), A(5), A(9), and A(12).
