(b) When is the reservoir's volume greatest, and what is that volume? Justify via A' and the candidates comparison.
(c) The local water authority claims the reservoir never dropped below 110 acre-feet during the 12 days. Evaluate the claim.
rubric: (b) A' = f: + on (0,5), − on (5,9), + on (9,12); candidates t = 5 (max from sign change) vs endpoint t = 12: A(5) = 140 > 125
Greatest volume 140 acre-feet at t = 5
(c) Minimum candidates: t = 0 (100) and t = 9 (115); A(0) = 100 < 110 — claim false at the start
frq.model_answer: (a) A(0) = 100. A(5) = 100 + 40 = 140. A(9) = 140 - 25 = 115. A(12) = 115 + 10 = 125. (b) A'(t) = f(t) by the Fundamental Theorem. A rises on (0, 5), falls on (5, 9), rises on (9, 12) — local max at t = 5. Comparing with the right endpoint: A(5) = 140 versus A(12) = 125: the reservoir is fullest at t = 5 with 140 acre-feet. (c) The volume's minimum candidates are the left endpoint and the − to + turn at t = 9: A(0) = 100 and A(9) = 115. Since A(0) = 100 < 110, the claim is false — though only barely, and only at the very start: from the moment inflow began, the reservoir stayed above 110 after recovering past it early in the window. More precisely, A starts at 100, so 'never below 110' fails at t = 0 itself.

subject: AP Calculus BC
chapter_title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus — Part 2 and Antiderivatives
hook: Part 2 is the payoff: to evaluate any definite integral, find an antiderivative, plug in the endpoints, subtract. Centuries of area problems collapse into algebra — provided you can run differentiation backward, which is this chapter's craft.
learning_objectives: State and apply FTC Part 2: ∫ₐᵇ f = F(b) - F(a) for any antiderivative F
Build the basic antiderivative library by reversing the derivative rules
Use the +C correctly in indefinite integrals and drop it correctly in definite ones
Evaluate definite integrals of polynomials, powers, trig, exponentials, and 1/x
Solve initial-value problems: recover f from f' and a point

sections.title: Part 2 and the Evaluation Ritual
sections.subtitle: F(b) minus F(a)
sections.body:
FTC Part 2: if F is ANY antiderivative of the continuous function f (meaning F' = f), then ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a). The notation [F(x)]ₐᵇ packages the ritual: antidifferentiate, evaluate at the top, evaluate at the bottom, subtract. The connection to Part 1: the accumulation ∫ₐˣ f IS an antiderivative, and any two antiderivatives differ by a constant that cancels in the subtraction — so any antiderivative works.

The ritual, run: ∫₁³ x² dx = [x³/3]₁³ = 27/3 - 1/3 = 26/3. The rectangle limits of chapter 2 would labor for this; the algebra takes one line. That collapse — geometry into algebra — is why the theorem carries the name Fundamental.

Why no +C in definite integrals: include it and watch it cancel — (F(b) + C) - (F(a) + C) = F(b) - F(a). The constant is genuine bookkeeping for INDEFINITE integrals (next section) and pure decoration in definite ones. Writing it in definite evaluations is harmless but signals confusion; omitting it in indefinite answers loses a point.

Sign discipline in the subtraction: F(b) - F(a) with the TOP bound first, and parentheses around negative evaluations — ∫₋₂¹ x³ dx = [x⁴/4] = 1/4 - 16/4 = -15/4, where sloppy minus-handling routinely flips answers. The evaluation bar is the unit's highest-volume arithmetic; protect it with parentheses.
key_terms: ∫ₐᵇ f = F(b) - F(a) for any F with F' = f
Any antiderivative works — the +C dies in the subtraction
boxes: ap_alert

Calculator-section integrals can be evaluated numerically — but the no-calculator section's definite integrals are exactly this ritual, and arithmetic slips in F(b) - F(a) (especially with negative bounds and even powers) outnumber concept errors three to one. Parentheses around every substituted value.

sections.title: The Antiderivative Library
sections.subtitle: Differentiation's table, reversed
sections.body:
Every derivative fact reads backward as an antiderivative fact. The power rule reverses to ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C for n ≠ -1 — raise the power, divide by the new power. The excluded case n = -1 is the logarithm's seat: ∫(1/x) dx = ln|x| + C, the absolute value extending the formula to negative x (where 1/x still demands an antiderivative and ln|x| supplies it).

Trig reverses with signs to mind: ∫cos = sin + C; ∫sin = -cos + C (the minus, because (cos)' = -sin); ∫sec² = tan + C; ∫sec·tan = sec + C; ∫csc² = -cot + C; ∫csc·cot = -csc + C. Exponentials: ∫eˣ = eˣ + C; ∫bˣ = bˣ/ln b + C. The inverse-trig pair from Unit 3, now in their destined role: ∫dx/(1 + x²) = arctan x + C and ∫dx/√(1 - x²) = arcsin x + C.

Linearity carries over wholesale: antidifferentiate term by term, constants ride along. ∫(6x² - 4 sin x + 5/x) dx = 2x³ + 4 cos x + 5 ln|x| + C — one C suffices for the whole expression (the constants merge). Rewriting before integrating is the same discipline as differentiating: √x → x^{1/2} → (2/3)x^{3/2}, and 1/x⁴ → x⁻⁴ → -x⁻³/3.

Verification is uniquely cheap in this direction: DIFFERENTIATE your answer and watch for the integrand. Antidifferentiation guesses are self-grading — a ten-second derivative check converts uncertainty into proof, and the habit catches sign slips (the ∫sin minus!) before they cost.
key_terms: ∫xⁿ = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + C, n ≠ -1; the gap at -1 belongs to ln|x|
∫sin = -cos + C: antiderivative signs flip where derivative signs flipped
Check every antiderivative by differentiating it — self-grading work
boxes: ap_alert

∫(1/x) dx = ln|x| + C — the absolute value is graded on the AP. Omitting it on integrals whose interval is positive is tolerated; omitting it in general answers or on intervals touching negatives is a deduction. Write |x| by default.

sections.title: Initial Value Problems
sections.subtitle: Pinning down the +C
sections.body:
The indefinite integral's +C encodes a family: all vertical shifts of one antiderivative. An INITIAL CONDITION — one known point — selects the family member. Given f'(x) = 3x² - 4 with f(1) = 5: antidifferentiate to f(x) = x³ - 4x + C, substitute the point: 5 = 1 - 4 + C, so C = 8 and f(x) = x³ - 4x + 8. Antidifferentiate, substitute, solve, write the finished function — the four-beat IVP ritual.

Motion is the genre's home turf: given acceleration a(t) = -32 ft/s² (gravity), v(0) = 64, s(0) = 80 — antidifferentiate twice, pinning a constant at each level. v(t) = -32t + C₁ with v(0) = 64: v = -32t + 64. s(t) = -16t² + 64t + C₂ with s(0) = 80: s = -16t² + 64t + 80. Projectile problems, fully armed: when does it peak (v = 0), how high (s there), when does it land (s = 0).

The FTC alternative phrasing — f(b) = f(a) + ∫ₐᵇ f' — solves IVPs without naming C: f(3) = f(1) + ∫₁³ (3x² - 4) dx = 5 + [x³ - 4x]₁³ = 5 + (15 - (-3)) = 23. When only ONE value is wanted (not the whole formula), the accumulation route is faster and calculator-friendly; when the formula is wanted, the C-route delivers it. Both phrasings are the same mathematics; fluency means choosing by what the question requests.

Two-constant problems flag a BC reflex: each antidifferentiation level needs its own condition, and conditions can arrive at different points (v(2) = 10, s(0) = 3) — substitute each at ITS point, in order. The bookkeeping is trivial when organized level by level and a mess when interleaved.
key_terms: f' plus one point determines f: antidifferentiate, substitute, solve for C
a → v → s, one constant pinned per level
f(b) = f(a) + ∫ₐᵇ f': the C-free route to single values
boxes: ap_alert

When an FRQ gives f' and f(a) and asks only for f(b), skip the C entirely: f(b) = f(a) + ∫ₐᵇ f' dx, evaluated (by hand or calculator as the section permits). The accumulation route is faster, C-error-proof, and worth the same full credit.

sections.title: Hypotheses and Honest Limits
sections.subtitle: Where Part 2 can fail, and graph-based evaluation
sections.body:
Part 2's hypothesis — f continuous on [a, b] — is not decoration. The cautionary classic: ∫₋₁¹ (1/x²) dx 'evaluated' as [-1/x]₋₁¹ = -1 - 1 = -2. A negative area for a positive function: absurd. The failure: 1/x² is discontinuous (unbounded) at 0, inside the interval; the theorem never applied, and the integral is in fact improper (chapter 8's subject) and divergent. Scan the interval for discontinuities BEFORE invoking the ritual.

Piecewise integrands route around their seams by splitting: ∫₀⁴ f with f defined piecewise at x = 2 becomes ∫₀² + ∫₂⁴, each piece evaluated by its own formula. Absolute-value integrands are the recurring case: for ∫₀⁴ |x - 2| dx, split at the corner x = 2: ∫₀² (2 - x) dx + ∫₂⁴ (x - 2) dx = 2 + 2 = 4. Splitting at the kink converts one impossible antiderivative into two trivial ones.

When no elementary antiderivative exists (e^{-x²}, sin(x²), the unit's recurring guests), Part 2 is not wrong but UNAVAILABLE — evaluation falls back to geometry (chapter 1), numerics (chapter 2), the calculator (on active sections), or stays symbolic as an accumulation function (chapter 3). Knowing WHICH tool a given integral admits is itself the tested skill: the exam mixes evaluable and non-evaluable integrands deliberately.

The unit's arc from here: the library handles integrands that LOOK like derivative-table entries. Most integrands don't — they look like chain-rule outputs (u-substitution, next), product-rule outputs (integration by parts), or rational functions (partial fractions). The remaining chapters are pattern-recognition training: which derivative rule, run backward, unlocks each integrand family.
key_terms: Discontinuities inside [a, b] void the ritual — check before evaluating
Piecewise and absolute-value integrands integrate piece by piece
Geometry, numerics, FTC, or symbolic accumulation — matched to the integrand
boxes: ap_alert

∫|expression| dx ALWAYS splits at the expression's zeros — there is no antiderivative of an absolute value in one piece. The split-point computation is the question's actual content; the two resulting integrals are routine.

mcq.question: ∫₁⁴ (2x - 3) dx =
∫ (4/x) dx =
mcq.explanation: Constant out, reciprocal integrates to ln|x|: 4 ln|x| + C. (C lacks both the absolute value and the constant.)

mcq.question: ∫₀^{π/2} sin x dx =
f'(x) = 6x² + 2 and f(1) = 4. Then f(x) =

choices.C: Both A and B describe f(x) = 2x³ + 2x

mcq.explanation: f = 2x³ + 2x + C; 4 = 2 + 2 + C gives C = 0, so f(x) = 2x³ + 2x.

mcq.question: A correct evaluation of ∫₀⁶ |x - 4| dx requires
mcq.explanation: Absolute values split at their zeros: triangles of area 8 and 2, total 10. No one-piece antiderivative of |x - 4| exists.

frq.question:
Evaluate the following, showing antiderivatives and the evaluation bar.
(a) ∫₁⁸ 3·x^{1/3} dx
(b) ∫_{π/4}^{π/2} (2 cos x - csc² x) dx
(c) ∫₁ᵉ (4/x + 2x) dx
rubric: All three carried out with the bar and clean substitution

frq.question:
A ball is thrown upward from a 96-foot building with initial velocity 16 ft/s; acceleration is a(t) = -32 ft/s².
(a) Find v(t) and s(t).
(b) Find the maximum height, with justification that it is a maximum.
(c) Find the speed at the moment of impact with the ground.
rubric: (b) v = 0 at t = ½; s(½) = -4 + 8 + 96 = 100 ft; v changes + to − (or s'' < 0): maximum
Speed |v(3)| = 80 ft/s
frq.model_answer: (a) v(t) = ∫a dt = -32t + C₁ with v(0) = 16: v(t) = -32t + 16. s(t) = ∫v dt = -16t² + 16t + C₂ with s(0) = 96: s(t) = -16t² + 16t + 96. (b) v(t) = 0 at t = ½ s. v changes from positive to negative there (linear with negative slope), so s has its maximum: s(½) = -4 + 8 + 96 = 100 feet. (c) Impact: s(t) = 0 ⟹ -16(t² - t - 6) = 0 ⟹ (t - 3)(t + 2) = 0 ⟹ t = 3 s. v(3) = -96 + 16 = -80 ft/s — moving downward at impact, with speed |−80| = 80 ft/s.

frq.question:
Let f be continuous with f(2) = 7, and suppose f'(x) = 6x² - 10x for all x.
(a) Find f(x) using an initial value computation.
(b) Recompute f(4) using the accumulation form f(4) = f(2) + ∫₂⁴ f'(x) dx, and confirm the two routes agree.
(c) Explain why the two routes must always agree, referencing the appropriate part of the Fundamental Theorem.
rubric: Direct check: f(4) = 128 - 80 + 11 = 59 ✓
(c) FTC Part 2: ∫₂⁴ f' = f(4) - f(2) for any antiderivative — the accumulation IS the net change
frq.model_answer: (a) f(x) = 2x³ - 5x² + C. The condition: 7 = 2(8) - 5(4) + C = -4 + C, so C = 11 and f(x) = 2x³ - 5x² + 11. (b) ∫₂⁴ (6x² - 10x) dx = [2x³ - 5x²]₂⁴ = (128 - 80) - (16 - 20) = 48 - (-4) = 52. So f(4) = 7 + 52 = 59. Direct: f(4) = 128 - 80 + 11 = 59 ✓. (c) FTC Part 2 states ∫₂⁴ f'(x) dx = f(4) - f(2) — the definite integral of a rate is exactly the net change of the function. Adding f(2) to both sides gives the accumulation form, so the C-route and the accumulation route are algebraic rearrangements of the same theorem; they cannot disagree.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: Most integrands aren't in the library — they're chain-rule outputs wearing disguises. u-Substitution is the chain rule run backward: spot the inside function, watch its derivative cancel, and a hopeless integral becomes a one-line lookup.
learning_objectives: Identify integrands of the form f(g(x))·g'(x) suitable for substitution
Execute the substitution ritual: choose u, compute du, rewrite, integrate, back-substitute
Change the bounds of definite integrals to u-values and never return to x
Handle constant-adjustment substitutions where du differs by a factor
Recognize the ln|u| pattern for integrands shaped like u'/u

sections.title: The Chain Rule, Reversed
sections.subtitle: Spotting the inside function
sections.body:
Differentiating F(g(x)) produces f(g(x))·g'(x) — a composition times the inside's derivative. So any integrand with that anatomy antidifferentiates by recognizing it: ∫f(g(x))·g'(x) dx = F(g(x)) + C. u-Substitution mechanizes the recognition: set u = g(x), compute du = g'(x) dx, and the integral REWRITES as ∫f(u) du — a library problem in the u-world.

The showcase: ∫2x(x² + 3)⁴ dx. The inside is x² + 3; its derivative 2x sits right there as a factor. Let u = x² + 3, du = 2x dx: the integral becomes ∫u⁴ du = u⁵/5 + C = (x² + 3)⁵/5 + C. Differentiate to verify: 5·(x²+3)⁴/5 · 2x ✓ — the chain rule regenerates the integrand, confirming the whole philosophy.

What to choose as u: the INSIDE of the composition — the expression under a power, inside a trig function, in an exponent, under a root. The litmus test: after computing du, the REST of the integrand should disappear into it. If x-stuff survives the substitution, the choice failed; pick again or suspect another technique.

The dx is not decoration: du = g'(x) dx is a complete package (the differentials from Unit 4's linearization chapter, earning their keep), and every x and dx must convert to u and du before integrating. A half-converted integral — u's and x's cohabiting — is meaningless and ungradable; the rewrite is all-or-nothing.
key_terms: Set u = inside, du = u' dx; rewrite wholly in u; integrate; back-substitute
f(g(x))·g'(x): composition present, inside's derivative available as a factor
No x may survive into the u-integral — mixed-variable integrals are meaningless
boxes: ap_alert

Choose u so that du is VISIBLY waiting in the integrand: in ∫x e^{x²} dx, u = x² works because du = 2x dx matches the loose x (up to the constant 2). If no candidate u has its derivative on site, u-substitution is the wrong tool — move on.

sections.title: Constant Adjustment
sections.subtitle: When du is off by a factor
sections.body:
Usually the integrand carries ALMOST du: ∫x e^{x²} dx has u = x², du = 2x dx, but only x dx appears — half of du. Constants are no obstacle: x dx = du/2, so the integral is ∫e^u (du/2) = e^u/2 + C = e^{x²}/2 + C. Solve du's equation for the piece you actually have, and the constant rides outside.

The canonical small cases live here: ∫cos(3x) dx with u = 3x gives sin(3x)/3 + C; ∫e^{5x} dx = e^{5x}/5 + C; ∫(2x + 7)⁹ dx = (2x + 7)¹⁰/20 + C. Linear insides ax + b always cost a factor of 1/a — a pattern worth automating since it covers a third of all exam substitutions.

What constant adjustment can NEVER do: manufacture missing VARIABLES. ∫e^{x²} dx (no loose x) does not yield to u = x² — du = 2x dx demands an x the integrand lacks, and no constant fixes a missing variable. That integral has no elementary antiderivative at all; recognizing the difference between off-by-a-constant (fixable) and off-by-a-variable (fatal) is a graded discrimination.

The u'/u pattern deserves its own reflex: any integrand shaped like derivative-over-function integrates to ln|function|. ∫x/(x² + 1) dx: u = x² + 1 catches du = 2x dx, giving ½ln(x² + 1) + C. ∫tan x dx = ∫sin x/cos x dx with u = cos x: -ln|cos x| + C = ln|sec x| + C — the tangent integral, derived in one substitution and worth memorizing as a result.
key_terms: x dx = du/2 and friends — solve du's equation for what you have
Derivative-over-function integrates to ln of the function — tan x's secret
boxes: ap_alert

Constants adjust; variables don't. ∫x e^{x²} dx submits to u-substitution, ∫e^{x²} dx does not — and the exam pairs them deliberately. The presence or absence of the loose x is the entire question; check it before committing.

sections.title: Definite Integrals: Change the Bounds
sections.subtitle: Move to u-world and stay there
sections.body:
For definite integrals, convert the BOUNDS along with everything else: when u = g(x), the x-bounds a, b become u-bounds g(a), g(b), and the evaluation finishes entirely in u. ∫₀² x√(x² + 1) dx: u = x² + 1, du = 2x dx; bounds x = 0 → u = 1, x = 2 → u = 5. The integral is ½∫₁⁵ √u du = ½·(2/3)u^{3/2}|₁⁵ = (5√5 - 1)/3. No back-substitution, no returning to x — the bounds did the conversion permanently.

The alternative — keeping x-bounds, back-substituting, then evaluating — is legal but slower and traps the unwary who plug x-values into u-expressions. The AP convention rewards bound-changing: write the new bounds ON the integral sign at the rewrite step, and the work self-documents. Mixed notation (u-integrand with x-bounds) is ambiguous and costs presentation points.

Bound order can FLIP under decreasing substitutions: u = cos x on [0, π/2] sends the bounds to 1 and 0 — the u-integral runs from 1 to 0, and reversing it (with the sign flip from chapter 1's properties) tidies the evaluation. The flip is not an error; it is the substitution being honest about direction. ∫₀^{π/2} sin x cos⁴x dx: u = cos x, du = -sin x dx: -∫₁⁰ u⁴ du = ∫₀¹ u⁴ du = 1/5.

Symmetry dividends arrive free in u-world: substitutions sometimes reveal that a definite integral's u-version has equal bounds (instant zero) or symmetric bounds with an odd integrand (also zero). The bounds carry information; converting them early lets that information surface before any antiderivative work.
key_terms: x-bounds map through u = g(x): evaluate wholly in u-world
New bounds written on the integral at the substitution step
Decreasing u reverses bound order; the sign-flip property restores it
boxes: ap_alert

The classic definite-substitution error: rewriting ∫₀² ... dx as ∫ u⁴ du and then evaluating at 0 and 2 — the OLD x-bounds — in the u-antiderivative. Changing the bounds at the moment of substitution makes the error structurally impossible. Change them every time.

sections.title: Substitution Judgment
sections.subtitle: Recognition drills and rearrangement tricks
sections.body:
Fluency is recognizing the family fast. Powers of an inside: (x³ + 1)⁷·x² dx — u = x³ + 1. Exponentials of an inside: e^{sin x}cos x dx — u = sin x. Roots of an inside: x√(x² - 4) — u = x² - 4. Trig of an inside: sec²(5x) — linear inside. Derivative-over-function: (2x + 3)/(x² + 3x) — u'/u, instant logarithm. Five patterns cover the AP's substitution menu nearly completely.

The rearrangement trick for stubborn leftovers: ∫x√(x - 1) dx with u = x - 1 leaves a loose x — but x = u + 1 converts it: ∫(u + 1)√u du = ∫(u^{3/2} + u^{1/2}) du = (2/5)u^{5/2} + (2/3)u^{3/2} + C, back-substituted. When u's equation can be SOLVED for the leftover x, the substitution survives; this 'back-solve' extension handles the linear-inside-with-extra-x family the exam likes.

When substitution fails, the diagnosis matters: a PRODUCT of unrelated functions (x·sin x — no composition anywhere) signals integration by parts, next chapter. A RATIONAL function with factorable denominator signals partial fractions, the chapter after. The techniques partition the integrand world; mis-routing wastes minutes, and the routing cue is structural (composition? product? ratio?) exactly like Unit 3's dispatch algorithm for derivatives.

Verification stays cheap: differentiate the answer. Every substitution result, indefinite or definite-by-antiderivative, self-checks in ten seconds via the chain rule — which is, after all, what u-substitution was the whole time.
key_terms: Power, exponential, root, trig of an inside, plus u'/u — the recognition set
Leftover x converts via x = (solve u's equation): handles x√(x-1)
Composition → substitution; bare product → parts; factorable ratio → partial fractions
boxes: ap_alert

Five-second routing scan before integrating anything: is there a composition with its inside's derivative nearby (u-sub)? A product of unrelated pieces (parts)? A rational function (partial fractions or u'/u)? The scan assigns the tool; tools misassigned cost double time.

mcq.question: ∫ 2x(x² + 3)⁴ dx =
mcq.explanation: u = x² + 3 absorbs the 2x dx exactly: ∫u⁴ du = u⁵/5 + C.

mcq.question: ∫ x e^{x²} dx =
mcq.explanation: u = x²: x dx = du/2, giving ½∫eᵘ du = e^{x²}/2 + C.

mcq.question: ∫₀² x√(x² + 1) dx =
∫ (2x + 3)/(x² + 3x + 7) dx =
mcq.explanation: The numerator is exactly the denominator's derivative: u'/u integrates to ln|u|.

mcq.question: Which integral CANNOT be evaluated by u-substitution (or any elementary method)?
mcq.explanation: u = x² demands an x-factor for du; B and C have it (up to constants), D has a linear inside. A is missing the variable — no elementary antiderivative exists.

frq.question:
Evaluate each integral, showing the substitution, the du equation, and (where definite) the converted bounds.
(a) ∫ sec²(4x) dx
(b) ∫₀^{π/2} sin x cos⁴x dx
(c) ∫₁² x/(x² + 1) dx
rubric: (a) u = 4x: tan(4x)/4 + C
(b) u = cos x, du = -sin x dx, bounds 1 → 0; -∫₁⁰ u⁴ du = ∫₀¹ u⁴ du = 1/5
(c) u = x² + 1, bounds 2 → 5: ½∫₂⁵ du/u = ½(ln 5 - ln 2) = ½ln(5/2)
Bounds converted at the substitution step in (b) and (c)
frq.model_answer: (a) u = 4x, du = 4 dx: ∫sec²u (du/4) = tan(u)/4 + C = tan(4x)/4 + C. (b) u = cos x, du = -sin x dx; bounds: x = 0 → u = 1, x = π/2 → u = 0. The integral becomes -∫₁⁰ u⁴ du = ∫₀¹ u⁴ du = [u⁵/5]₀¹ = 1/5. (c) u = x² + 1, du = 2x dx; bounds: x = 1 → u = 2, x = 2 → u = 5. The integral is ½∫₂⁵ du/u = ½[ln u]₂⁵ = ½(ln 5 - ln 2) = ½ ln(5/2).

frq.question:
Consider ∫ x√(x - 1) dx.
(a) Explain why the naive substitution u = x - 1 appears to fail, and how the back-solve x = u + 1 rescues it.
(b) Complete the integration.
(c) Verify your answer by differentiation.
rubric: (a) u = x - 1 leaves a loose x; since x = u + 1, the leftover converts exactly
(b) ∫(u + 1)u^{1/2} du = (2/5)u^{5/2} + (2/3)u^{3/2} + C, back-substituted with u = x - 1
Factoring step in the verification shown
frq.model_answer: (a) With u = x - 1, du = dx, but the integrand keeps a factor of x not covered by du — normally fatal. However, u's equation solves for it: x = u + 1, converting every leftover. (b) ∫(u + 1)√u du = ∫(u^{3/2} + u^{1/2}) du = (2/5)u^{5/2} + (2/3)u^{3/2} + C = (2/5)(x-1)^{5/2} + (2/3)(x-1)^{3/2} + C. (c) Differentiating: (x-1)^{3/2} + (x-1)^{1/2}. Factor out (x-1)^{1/2}: (x-1)^{1/2}[(x-1) + 1] = x(x-1)^{1/2} = x√(x-1) ✓ — the original integrand.

frq.question:
The rate of oil leakage from a tanker is R(t) = 50t e^{-t²/8} liters per hour, t in hours.
(a) Find the total oil leaked from t = 0 to t = 2 using a substitution with converted bounds.
(b) Find the time at which the leakage RATE is greatest, using Unit 5 machinery on R.
(c) Total leakage over all time would be ∫₀^∞ R dt — name the chapter-ahead concept this integral requires, and explain in one sentence why the bound ∞ demands new machinery.
rubric: (b) R' = 50e^{-t²/8}(1 - t²/4) = 0 → t = 2; sign change + to −: maximum at t = 2
(c) Improper integral
Reason: ∞ is not a number to substitute — the integral is defined as a limit of finite-bound integrals
frq.model_answer: (a) Let u = t²/8, du = (t/4) dt, so t dt = 4 du; bounds t = 0 → u = 0, t = 2 → u = 1/2. ∫₀² 50 t e^{-t²/8} dt = 50·4∫₀^{1/2} e^{-u} du = 200[-e^{-u}]₀^{1/2} = 200(1 - e^{-1/2}) ≈ 78.7 liters. (b) R'(t) = 50e^{-t²/8} + 50t·e^{-t²/8}·(-t/4) = 50e^{-t²/8}(1 - t²/4). The exponential never vanishes; 1 - t²/4 = 0 at t = 2, with R' changing + to − there: the leak rate peaks at t = 2 hours. (c) ∫₀^∞ R dt is an IMPROPER integral. Infinity is not a number that can be substituted into an antiderivative — the integral must be defined as lim b→∞ ∫₀ᵇ R dt, the limit machinery of this unit's final chapter.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: BC ONLY — and worth the price of admission: integration by parts is the product rule run backward, the only tool that integrates x·eˣ, x·cos x, and ln x itself. One formula, one choosing-rule, and a whole family of integrals falls.
learning_objectives: Derive the parts formula ∫u dv = uv - ∫v du from the product rule
Choose u by the LIATE priority and dv as the rest
Apply parts iteratively for powers like x² eˣ
Integrate ln x and other lone awkward functions via dv = dx
Execute the boundary-term bookkeeping for definite integrals

sections.title: The Product Rule, Reversed
sections.subtitle: Deriving ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du
sections.body:
Integrate the product rule (uv)' = u'v + uv' across an interval: uv = ∫u'v + ∫uv'. Rearranged: ∫u v' dx = uv - ∫u' v dx, or in differential shorthand, ∫u dv = uv - ∫v du. Integration by parts trades one integral for another — and the entire craft is making the trade FAVORABLE: ∫v du should be simpler than ∫u dv.

The showcase: ∫x eˣ dx. Choose u = x (differentiates to the simpler 1) and dv = eˣ dx (integrates without getting worse, to v = eˣ). The formula: ∫x eˣ dx = x eˣ - ∫eˣ·1 dx = x eˣ - eˣ + C = (x - 1)eˣ + C. The x DIED under differentiation — that is the trade working: polynomial factors are mortal, and parts kills them one differentiation at a time.

The bookkeeping layout that prevents chaos: a 2×2 box — u and dv on top, du and v below — filled before touching the formula. u = x, dv = eˣ dx; du = dx, v = eˣ. Then transcribe: uv minus the integral of v du. The box is to parts what the skeleton was to the quotient rule: structure that survives exam pressure.

No +C appears when computing v from dv — any antiderivative works (the constant would cancel through the formula, same argument as FTC2), so take the cleanest one. The final answer carries one +C, attached at the end.
key_terms: ∫u dv = uv - ∫v du: the product rule integrated and rearranged
Choose so ∫v du is SIMPLER — typically u dies under differentiation
u, dv / du, v — filled completely before invoking the formula
boxes: ap_alert

Parts is BC-only material and the exam flags it with unmistakable integrands: x eˣ, x sin x, x ln x, ln x alone, arctan x alone. Polynomial-times-transcendental is the silhouette; when you see it, draw the box.

sections.title: Choosing u: LIATE
sections.subtitle: The priority list that almost never fails
sections.body:
The choice of u decides everything, and the LIATE mnemonic ranks candidates: Logarithmic, Inverse trig, Algebraic (polynomials), Trigonometric, Exponential — choose u as the EARLIEST type present; dv swallows the rest. Logs and inverse trig differentiate beautifully (to algebraic functions) but integrate painfully, so they grab u; exponentials integrate without complaint, so they accept dv.

Run the list: ∫x cos x dx — Algebraic beats Trig: u = x, dv = cos x dx, giving x sin x - ∫sin x dx = x sin x + cos x + C. ∫x ln x dx — Log beats Algebraic: u = ln x, dv = x dx: (x²/2)ln x - ∫(x²/2)(1/x) dx = (x²/2)ln x - x²/4 + C. The ranking inverts naive instinct (the ln, not the x, takes u) and that inversion is exactly what LIATE encodes.

Why LIATE works, in one sentence: it orders functions from 'differentiates-much-simpler' to 'integrates-without-damage' — u wants the former, dv needs the latter. Understanding the principle lets you sanity-check the mnemonic on hybrids and trust departures from it in the rare cases (none on the AP) where it misleads.

The wrong choice diagnoses itself: picking u = eˣ in ∫x eˣ dx produces ∫v du = ∫(x²/2)eˣ dx — WORSE than the start. A trade that complicates is a signal to swap the roles, not to push harder. One failed box costs thirty seconds; recognizing the failure fast is part of the skill.
key_terms: Log, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential — u takes the earliest type present
u should simplify under d/dx; dv must integrate without damage
If ∫v du is worse than the original, swap the choice and rerun
boxes: ap_alert

∫ln x dx — a lone logarithm — is the LIATE edge case the exam loves: u = ln x and dv = dx (yes, just dx). Then v = x and the formula gives x ln x - ∫x·(1/x) dx = x ln x - x + C. The dv = dx move also integrates arctan x; memorize the maneuver.

sections.title: Iteration and the Definite Version
sections.subtitle: Higher powers, boundary terms
sections.body:
Powers above one need repeated parts: ∫x² eˣ dx with u = x² gives x² eˣ - 2∫x eˣ dx — the remaining integral is last section's showcase, yielding x² eˣ - 2(x - 1)eˣ + C = (x² - 2x + 2)eˣ + C. Each round kills one power; xⁿ needs n rounds. The discipline: keep LIATE's choice (algebraic stays u) consistent through every round — swapping mid-stream undoes the previous round's progress exactly.

Definite integrals carry the boundary term through: ∫ₐᵇ u dv = [uv]ₐᵇ - ∫ₐᵇ v du. The uv piece evaluates at the bounds IMMEDIATELY — it is a number — while the remaining integral proceeds. ∫₁ᵉ ln x dx = [x ln x]₁ᵉ - ∫₁ᵉ dx = (e·1 - 1·0) - (e - 1) = e - e + 1 = 1. A clean, exam-loved result: the area under ln from 1 to e is exactly 1.

The circular family closes the chapter's technique list: ∫eˣ sin x dx runs parts twice (either consistent choice) and reproduces ITSELF: ∫eˣ sin x dx = eˣ sin x - eˣ cos x - ∫eˣ sin x dx. The escape move: add the integral to both sides and divide by 2 — ∫eˣ sin x dx = eˣ(sin x - cos x)/2 + C. The 'solve for the integral' finale turns apparent circularity into the answer; it appears on BC exams as the hardest parts variant.

Tabular shorthand for the iterative cases: columns of repeated derivatives of u (down to zero) and repeated antiderivatives of dv, joined diagonally with alternating signs. For x² eˣ: derivatives x², 2x, 2, 0; antiderivatives eˣ, eˣ, eˣ; diagonals (+x²eˣ)(-2xeˣ)(+2eˣ) — the answer assembled without writing the formula once. Legal, fast, and self-checking against the longhand.
key_terms: xⁿ dies in n rounds; keep the LIATE roles fixed throughout
[uv]ₐᵇ evaluates immediately; only ∫v du continues as an integral
eˣ sin x: two rounds reproduce the integral — add and divide by 2
boxes: ap_alert

In the circular eˣ·trig cases, the second round must keep the SAME choice pattern as the first (exponential as dv both times, or trig as dv both times) — mixing undoes round one and returns the original integral with nothing gained. Consistency is the entire trick.

sections.title: Parts in Context
sections.subtitle: Where the technique lives on the exam
sections.body:
Routing review, now three techniques deep: composition with inside's derivative → u-substitution; product of UNRELATED functions (no composition) → parts; lone awkward function (ln x, arctan x) → parts with dv = dx. The x e^{x²} versus x eˣ pair is the canonical discrimination: the first has the composition anatomy (substitution, instantly), the second is a genuine unrelated product (parts). Thirty seconds of routing beats five minutes of wrong-tool grinding.

Applied integrals deliver parts in costume: expected values in probability (∫x·f(x) dx with exponential densities), work and center-of-mass integrals, and BC's own coming attractions — arc-length and surface integrals occasionally reduce to parts-able forms, and Taylor series remainders (Unit 10) are proved with iterated parts. The technique is infrastructure, not trivia.

Accumulation-function problems hybridize with FTC: given F(x) = ∫₀ˣ t cos t dt, find F(π) — run parts inside the accumulation: [t sin t + cos t]₀^π = (0 + (-1)) - (0 + 1) = -2. The FTC supplies the frame; parts supplies the antiderivative; the layered problem is BC's bread and butter.

A final calibration note: parts problems on the AP stay SHALLOW — one round, occasionally two, the ln x maneuver, rarely the circular case. Triple iterations and exotic choices live in textbooks, not on the exam. Master the box, LIATE, the dv = dx move, and the boundary term; that inventory covers every parts question the AP has asked in a decade.
key_terms: Substitution (composition), parts (product), dv = dx (lone awkward function)
The discrimination pair: composition anatomy versus genuine product
One-to-two rounds, ln x, boundary terms — the complete AP inventory
boxes: ap_alert

Before starting any parts computation on a definite integral, check whether the integrand is secretly a u-substitution: ∫x e^{x²} dx submits to u = x² in one line, and running parts on it instead is a time-loss the exam engineers deliberately. Composition check first, always.

mcq.question: ∫₁ᵉ ln x dx =
Which integral should be routed to u-SUBSTITUTION rather than parts?
mcq.explanation: x e^{x²} has the composition-plus-inside-derivative anatomy: u = x² finishes in one line. The others are genuine parts customers.

frq.question:
Let I = ∫ x² eˣ dx.
(a) Set up the first round of integration by parts with the LIATE-correct choice, and carry it through to the reduced integral.
(b) Complete the second round and state the final antiderivative.
(c) Verify your answer by differentiation.
rubric: (a) u = x², dv = eˣ dx: I = x² eˣ - 2∫x eˣ dx
(b) Second round on ∫x eˣ: (x - 1)eˣ; assembled: (x² - 2x + 2)eˣ + C
(c) Differentiates: (2x - 2)eˣ + (x² - 2x + 2)eˣ = x² eˣ ✓
Consistent u-choice across rounds
frq.model_answer: (a) LIATE: algebraic u = x², dv = eˣ dx; du = 2x dx, v = eˣ. I = x² eˣ - ∫eˣ·2x dx = x² eˣ - 2∫x eˣ dx. (b) For ∫x eˣ dx: u = x, dv = eˣ dx gives x eˣ - eˣ. So I = x² eˣ - 2(x eˣ - eˣ) + C = (x² - 2x + 2)eˣ + C. (c) d/dx[(x² - 2x + 2)eˣ] = (2x - 2)eˣ + (x² - 2x + 2)eˣ = (x² )eˣ = x² eˣ ✓.

frq.question:
Evaluate ∫₀^{π/2} x sin x dx.
(a) Run integration by parts with the boundary-term bookkeeping.
(b) Interpret the boundary term's value at each endpoint.
(c) A region under y = x sin x from 0 to π/2 is proposed as a machine part's cross-section. State its exact area from (a), and approximate it to three decimals.
rubric: (a) u = x, dv = sin x dx: [-x cos x]₀^{π/2} + ∫₀^{π/2} cos x dx
Boundary term: 0 at both ends (cos(π/2) = 0; x = 0 at the bottom); remaining integral [sin x]₀^{π/2} = 1
(b) Top end dies via cos(π/2) = 0, bottom via the factor x = 0
(c) Area exactly 1; approximation 1.000
frq.model_answer: (a) u = x, dv = sin x dx; du = dx, v = -cos x. ∫₀^{π/2} x sin x dx = [-x cos x]₀^{π/2} + ∫₀^{π/2} cos x dx = (-（π/2)·0 + 0·1) + [sin x]₀^{π/2} = 0 + 1 = 1. (b) The boundary term vanishes at BOTH ends for different reasons: at x = π/2 because cos(π/2) = 0, and at x = 0 because the factor x itself is zero — a small bookkeeping elegance worth noticing. (c) The exact area is 1 square unit; to three decimals, 1.000.

frq.question:
Let J = ∫ eˣ cos x dx.
(a) Apply integration by parts twice with a consistent choice, showing that J reappears on the right side.
(b) Solve the resulting equation for J.
(c) Use your result to evaluate ∫₀^{π} eˣ cos x dx exactly.
rubric: (a) u = cos x both rounds (or eˣ both rounds): J = eˣ cos x + ∫eˣ sin x = eˣ cos x + eˣ sin x - J
(b) 2J = eˣ(cos x + sin x): J = eˣ(sin x + cos x)/2 + C
Consistency of choice across rounds stated
frq.model_answer: (a) Round 1: u = cos x, dv = eˣ dx: J = eˣ cos x + ∫eˣ sin x dx. Round 2 (same pattern, u = sin x): ∫eˣ sin x dx = eˣ sin x - ∫eˣ cos x dx = eˣ sin x - J. Substituting: J = eˣ cos x + eˣ sin x - J. (b) 2J = eˣ(sin x + cos x), so J = eˣ(sin x + cos x)/2 + C. (c) ∫₀^π eˣ cos x dx = [eˣ(sin x + cos x)/2]₀^π = (e^π(0 + (-1)))/2 - (1(0 + 1))/2 = -e^π/2 - 1/2 = -(e^π + 1)/2.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: BC ONLY: a rational function that refuses every substitution splits — like a fraction into ½ + ⅓ — into pieces that each integrate to a logarithm. Partial fractions is algebra in service of integration, and the AP keeps its version mercifully tame.
learning_objectives: Decompose rational functions with distinct linear factors into partial fractions
Find the constants by the cover-up (root-substitution) method
Integrate each piece to its logarithm and assemble the answer
Divide first when the rational function is improper (top degree ≥ bottom degree)
Recognize the AP's boundaries: nonrepeating linear factors only

sections.title: Splitting the Fraction
sections.subtitle: Why and how the decomposition exists
sections.body:
The integrand 1/((x - 1)(x + 2)) defeats u-substitution (no factor's derivative is present) and parts (no useful product) — but it SPLITS: 1/((x - 1)(x + 2)) = A/(x - 1) + B/(x + 2) for the right constants A and B. Each piece is a u'/u-style logarithm-in-waiting; the decomposition converts one impossible integral into two trivial ones.

Why such constants exist: combining A/(x - 1) + B/(x + 2) over the common denominator gives (A(x + 2) + B(x - 1))/((x - 1)(x + 2)) — a numerator that is a general linear polynomial with two adjustable constants, enough freedom to match any constant or linear numerator. Distinct linear factors downstairs, one constant per factor upstairs: the template.

Finding A and B by clearing denominators: 1 = A(x + 2) + B(x - 1), an identity holding for ALL x. Substituting the roots makes terms vanish: x = 1 kills B's term — 1 = 3A, A = 1/3; x = -2 kills A's: 1 = -3B, B = -1/3. The root-substitution shortcut (the 'cover-up method') finds each constant in one line: cover the factor in the original fraction, evaluate the remainder at that factor's root.

The integration finale: ∫dx/((x-1)(x+2)) = (1/3)∫dx/(x-1) - (1/3)∫dx/(x+2) = (1/3)ln|x-1| - (1/3)ln|x+2| + C = (1/3)ln|(x-1)/(x+2)| + C. Decompose, integrate each piece, optionally consolidate the logs. Three beats, every time.
key_terms: Distinct linear factors split: one constant over each factor
Each constant = the original fraction with its factor covered, evaluated at that root
Each piece is c/(x - r): integrates to c·ln|x - r|
boxes: ap_alert

BC's partial fractions stay tame by design: DISTINCT LINEAR factors only — no repeated factors, no irreducible quadratics. If your decomposition seems to need A/(x-1)² or (Bx + C)/(x² + 1), re-read the problem; the AP didn't ask that.

sections.title: The Cover-Up Method, Drilled
sections.subtitle: Constants in one line each
sections.body:
The cover-up method formalized: to find the constant over (x - r), delete ('cover') that factor from the original fraction's denominator and evaluate what remains at x = r. For (3x + 5)/((x + 1)(x + 3)): the constant over (x + 1) is (3x + 5)/(x + 3) at x = -1: 2/2 = 1; over (x + 3): (3x + 5)/(x + 1) at x = -3: -4/(-2) = 2. Decomposition: 1/(x + 1) + 2/(x + 3). Integral: ln|x + 1| + 2 ln|x + 3| + C.

Why it works is the clearing-denominators argument compressed: substituting the root into the cleared identity annihilates every term except the target constant's. The method is rigorous, not a trick — but verify once per exam anyway: recombine the pieces mentally (or check one x-value, like x = 0) to confirm the split. Thirty seconds, and decomposition errors die before they propagate into logarithms.

Three-factor versions scale linearly: (x + 7)/((x)(x - 2)(x + 1)) gets three constants, each by one cover-up. The arithmetic multiplies, the method doesn't change. The exam's appetite stops at two or three factors; beyond that is textbook territory.

Definite versions assemble bounds onto the logs: ∫₃⁵ dx/((x - 1)(x + 2)) = (1/3)[ln|x - 1| - ln|x + 2|]₃⁵ = (1/3)[(ln 4 - ln 7) - (ln 2 - ln 5)] = (1/3)ln(10/7) after log algebra. Exact-form answers with consolidated logarithms are the expected presentation — decimal conversions only when the question asks.
key_terms: Cover the factor, evaluate at its root — one constant per line
Recombine or spot-check one x-value before integrating
ln a - ln b = ln(a/b): definite answers compress to single logarithms
boxes: ap_alert

After the cover-up, sanity-check SIGNS by recombining the first terms mentally: A/(x-1) + B/(x+2) should reproduce the original numerator's sign at a glance. Sign slips in cover-up arithmetic are the technique's only common failure mode.

sections.title: Improper Fractions Divide First
sections.subtitle: When the top is too big
sections.body:
Partial fractions demands a PROPER rational function — numerator degree strictly below denominator degree. When the top matches or exceeds the bottom, polynomial long division goes first: (x² + 3x + 5)/((x + 1)(x + 2)) = (x² + 3x + 5)/(x² + 3x + 2) divides to 1 + 3/((x + 1)(x + 2)) — a polynomial part plus a proper remainder fraction, each integrable by its own rules.

The polynomial part integrates trivially; the remainder decomposes as usual: 3/((x+1)(x+2)) = 3/(x+1) - 3/(x+2). Total: x + 3 ln|x+1| - 3 ln|x+2| + C. Divide, decompose, integrate — the full pipeline for any rational function in the AP's scope.

The degree check must be a reflex: scan top and bottom degrees BEFORE writing any A/(x - r) template. Decomposing an improper fraction produces unsolvable constant equations or wrong answers that look plausible — the failure is quiet, which is what makes the upfront check mandatory. Top degree ≥ bottom degree: divide. Always.

A BC connection ahead: the logistic differential equation (Unit 7) separates into exactly a partial-fractions integral — ∫dP/(P(L - P)) — and this chapter's technique is what solves it. Partial fractions is not an isolated trick; it is the algebra inside BC's most famous differential equation, which is reason enough for its place in the course.
key_terms: Numerator degree < denominator degree, or divide first
∫dP/(P(L - P)) — Unit 7's star equation runs on this chapter
boxes: ap_alert

Degree check FIRST: (x²+1)/((x-1)(x+2)) has equal degrees (2 and 2) and must be divided before decomposing. The improper-fraction trap is quiet — the A/B template seems to work and yields a wrong answer with no alarm. Make the check muscle memory.

sections.title: Routing, Completed
sections.subtitle: The integration decision tree, four techniques deep
sections.body:
The unit's decision tree, now complete for AP purposes: (1) Library form? Integrate directly. (2) Composition with the inside's derivative present (up to a constant)? u-Substitution. (3) u'/u shape specifically? Instant logarithm. (4) Product of unrelated functions, or a lone log/inverse-trig? Parts. (5) Rational function? Check degrees (divide if improper), check the denominator (factorable into distinct linear pieces?), then partial fractions. (6) None of the above on a no-calculator section? Re-examine — a rewrite (split the fraction, trig identity, completing nothing the AP needs) is hiding.

Discrimination practice across the rational family: ∫2x/(x² - 4) dx — the numerator IS the denominator's derivative: u'/u, instant ln|x² - 4|, NO decomposition needed. ∫dx/(x² - 4) — no derivative upstairs: partial fractions over (x-2)(x+2). ∫x²/(x² - 4) — improper: divide first. Three near-identical integrands, three different routes; the discrimination is the skill, and the exam tests it explicitly.

What stays outside the AP's fence, for orientation: repeated factors (A/(x-1) + B/(x-1)²), irreducible quadratics ((Bx + C)/(x² + 1)), trig substitution, and reduction formulas — college techniques the BC exam deliberately excludes. Knowing the fence keeps preparation focused and flags any practice problem demanding more as off-syllabus.

The unit closes one chapter from here: improper integrals extend the definite integral to infinite intervals and unbounded integrands — limits meeting accumulation, with the p-series criterion that Unit 10's convergence tests will lean on. The techniques are assembled; what remains is extending where integrals are allowed to live.
key_terms: Library, substitution, u'/u, parts, rational pipeline — the AP's full kit
u'/u vs partial fractions vs divide-first: near-twins, different routes
No repeated factors, no irreducible quadratics, no trig substitution
boxes: ap_alert

Before decomposing ANY rational integrand, check the numerator against the denominator's derivative: if they match up to a constant, u-substitution finishes in one line and decomposition is wasted effort. The u'/u check costs five seconds and is the most-skipped step in the unit.

frq.question:
Let f(x) = (x + 7)/((x - 1)(x + 3)).
(a) Decompose f into partial fractions using the cover-up method, showing each evaluation.
(b) Evaluate ∫₂⁴ f(x) dx, expressing the answer as a single logarithm.

rubric: Log algebra correct in (b)

frq.question:
Consider ∫ (x³ + 2x² - x - 3)/(x(x + 1)) dx. Note the numerator has degree 3 and the denominator degree 2.
(a) Perform the polynomial division to write the integrand as a polynomial plus a proper fraction, stating your quotient and remainder.
(b) Decompose the proper remainder fraction.
(c) Assemble the complete antiderivative.
rubric: (a) (x³ + 2x² - x - 3) ÷ (x² + x) = x + 1 remainder -2x - 3: integrand = x + 1 + (-2x - 3)/(x² + x)
(c) x²/2 + x - 3 ln|x| + ln|x + 1| + C
Division verified or stated with the remainder identity
frq.model_answer: (a) Dividing x³ + 2x² - x - 3 by x² + x: first term x (giving x³ + x²), subtract: x² - x - 3; next term 1 (giving x² + x), subtract: -2x - 3. So the integrand is x + 1 + (-2x - 3)/(x(x + 1)). (b) Cover-up on (-2x - 3)/(x(x + 1)): over x, evaluate at 0: -3/1 = -3; over (x + 1), at -1: (2 - 3)/(-1) = 1. Decomposition: -3/x + 1/(x + 1). (c) ∫ = x²/2 + x - 3 ln|x| + ln|x + 1| + C.

frq.question:
A population model leads to the integral ∫ dP/(P(100 - P)) (the logistic separation, previewing Unit 7).
(a) Decompose 1/(P(100 - P)) into partial fractions. (Treat P as the variable; note the second factor is (100 - P), whose root is P = 100.)
(b) Integrate, attending to the sign produced by the (100 - P) factor.
(c) Show the antiderivative can be written as (1/100) ln|P/(100 - P)| + C.
rubric: The minus sign from d/dP(100 - P) = -1 handled explicitly
frq.model_answer: (a) Cover-up: over P, evaluate 1/(100 - P) at P = 0: 1/100. Over (100 - P), evaluate 1/P at P = 100: 1/100. So 1/(P(100 - P)) = (1/100)[1/P + 1/(100 - P)]. (b) The first piece gives (1/100)ln|P|. The second: u = 100 - P has du = -dP, so ∫dP/(100 - P) = -ln|100 - P| — sign flip from the chain rule. Total: (1/100)ln|P| - (1/100)ln|100 - P| + C. (c) Combining the logs: (1/100)ln|P/(100 - P)| + C — exactly the form Unit 7's logistic solution will exponentiate.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: BC ONLY: can a region stretching to infinity have finite area? Sometimes — and the difference between 1/x and 1/x² at infinity is the difference between divergence and the number 1. Improper integrals are limits wearing integral signs, and they gatekeep all of Unit 10.
learning_objectives: Define improper integrals as limits of proper integrals, with mandatory limit notation
Evaluate infinite-bound integrals and determine convergence or divergence
Handle integrands with vertical asymptotes at or inside the bounds
Apply the p-test: ∫₁^∞ dx/xᵖ converges exactly when p > 1
Connect improper-integral convergence to the coming theory of infinite series

sections.title: Limits in Disguise
sections.subtitle: Defining the infinite-bound integral
sections.body:
∫₁^∞ f(x) dx is DEFINED as lim b→∞ ∫₁ᵇ f(x) dx: integrate to a finite cutoff b, then let the cutoff run away. If the limit exists (a finite number), the integral CONVERGES to it; if the limit is infinite or fails to exist, the integral DIVERGES. Infinity never enters an antiderivative — it enters a limit, afterward.

The headline pair: ∫₁^∞ dx/x² = lim b→∞ [-1/x]₁ᵇ = lim (1 - 1/b) = 1 — an infinite region with area exactly 1. But ∫₁^∞ dx/x = lim [ln x]₁ᵇ = lim ln b = ∞ — divergent. Both integrands die at infinity; 1/x just dies too slowly. Convergence is about the SPEED of decay, not the fact of it — the single most important intuition in the chapter and in Unit 10.

The notation is graded: writing ∫₁^∞ dx/x² = [-1/x]₁^∞ with ∞ 'plugged in' is a rubric deduction even when the answer is right. The required presentation: convert to lim b→∞ ∫₁ᵇ at the FIRST step, carry the b through the evaluation, take the limit LAST. Three visible stages — the AP grades the middle one specifically.

Doubly-infinite integrals split at any convenient point: ∫_{-∞}^∞ = ∫_{-∞}^0 + ∫₀^∞, each piece its own limit, and BOTH must converge for the whole to. The split discipline mirrors the piecewise splitting of chapter 4 — accumulation handles one frontier at a time.
key_terms: lim b→∞ ∫ₐᵇ f dx: a limit of proper integrals, never a plugged-in ∞
Finite limit: converges to it; infinite or nonexistent: diverges
1/x² converges, 1/x diverges — dying isn't enough; dying FAST enough is
boxes: ap_alert

The limit notation is a dedicated rubric point: 'lim b→∞' must appear BEFORE the antiderivative is evaluated, with b in the evaluation bar. The shortcut of plugging ∞ directly loses the point even with a correct final answer — every year, on every improper FRQ.

sections.title: The p-Test
sections.subtitle: The exact boundary of convergence
sections.body:
Generalizing the headline pair: ∫₁^∞ dx/xᵖ = lim b→∞ [x^{1-p}/(1-p)]₁ᵇ for p ≠ 1. The cutoff term b^{1-p} dies when 1 - p < 0 (p > 1) and explodes when p < 1; the case p = 1 is the logarithm, divergent. The p-TEST: ∫₁^∞ dx/xᵖ converges if and only if p > 1, and when it converges, its value is 1/(p - 1).

The boundary is strict and sharp: p = 1.0001 converges (to 10,000), p = 1 diverges, p = 0.9999 diverges. There is no fuzzy zone — and the same knife-edge will reappear verbatim as the p-series test in Unit 10, where Σ1/nᵖ obeys the identical criterion for the same underlying reason (the integral test will make the connection literal).

Worked contrasts cement it: ∫₁^∞ dx/x³ = 1/2 (p = 3 > 1 ✓). ∫₁^∞ dx/√x diverges (p = ½ < 1). ∫₁^∞ dx/x^{1.01} converges to 100 — barely over the line, finite all the same. Eyeballing the exponent against 1 routes the verdict in two seconds; the limit computation then certifies it for the rubric.

Exponential decay beats every power: ∫₀^∞ e^{-x} dx = lim [-e^{-x}]₀ᵇ = 1, and ∫₀^∞ e^{-kx} dx = 1/k for any k > 0. Exponentials at infinity are the friendliest integrands in the chapter — the growth hierarchy of Unit 1, now reading its decay-side consequences.
key_terms: ∫₁^∞ dx/xᵖ converges iff p > 1, to the value 1/(p - 1)
p = 1 diverges; any p > 1 converges — no fuzzy zone
∫₀^∞ e^{-kx} dx = 1/k: exponentials always converge at infinity
boxes: ap_alert

Memorize the p-test as stated — 'converges if and only if p > 1' — because Unit 10 reuses it for series verbatim, and the exam asks it in both costumes. The single criterion is worth points in two units.

sections.title: Vertical Asymptotes
sections.subtitle: When the integrand, not the bound, is infinite
sections.body:
The second improper species: a finite interval whose integrand blows up at an endpoint. ∫₀¹ dx/√x has a vertical asymptote at 0 — define it as lim a→0⁺ ∫ₐ¹ dx/√x = lim [2√x]ₐ¹ = lim (2 - 2√a) = 2. Convergent: the spike at zero is thin enough to enclose finite area. The one-sided limit approaches the singularity from inside the interval.

The endpoint p-test mirrors (and flips) the infinite-bound one: ∫₀¹ dx/xᵖ converges iff p < 1. At the singular end, SMALL p (gentle spikes) converges and large p diverges — the reverse of the behavior at infinity, because the danger zone is x near 0 where small powers are tamer. The pair of p-tests, with their opposite inequalities, is a classic discrimination question.

The hidden-singularity trap: ∫₋₁¹ dx/x² LOOKS routine, but the integrand explodes at x = 0 — inside the interval. The chapter-4 warning returns with teeth: evaluating [−1/x]₋₁¹ = -2 (negative, for a positive integrand!) is nonsense; the honest treatment splits at 0 into two improper integrals, each divergent — the integral diverges. Scanning the interval for interior singularities is mandatory before ANY evaluation bar.

Mixed cases chain the species: ∫₀^∞ dx/(√x(1 + x)) is improper at both ends, split at x = 1 into an endpoint-singular piece and an infinite-bound piece, each assessed separately. The AP keeps such doubles rare; the splitting principle is what it tests when they appear.
key_terms: lim a→r⁺ from inside: the one-sided limit version of improper
∫₀¹ dx/xᵖ converges iff p < 1 — opposite inequality at the spike
Blow-ups INSIDE the interval force a split; ignoring them yields nonsense
boxes: ap_alert

∫₋₁¹ dx/x² = -2 is the chapter's poison answer — negative area from a positive function, produced by ignoring the interior asymptote. Scan (a, b) for integrand blow-ups before every definite evaluation; the scan IS the question on several past exams.

sections.title: Convergence Without Evaluation
sections.subtitle: Comparison thinking and the bridge to series
sections.body:
Sometimes the verdict matters and the value doesn't — and comparison delivers verdicts without antiderivatives. If 0 ≤ f(x) ≤ g(x) for large x: g converging forces f to converge (trapped under a finite roof), and f diverging forces g to diverge (pushed up by an infinite floor). ∫₁^∞ dx/(x³ + 5): the integrand sits below 1/x³, whose integral converges (p = 3) — converges, no decomposition needed.

The comparison instinct: identify the integrand's DOMINANT behavior at the frontier (largest power downstairs minus upstairs, exponential factors), compare to the matching p-integral or exponential. (sin²x)/x² ≤ 1/x²: converges. (2 + cos x)/x ≥ 1/x: diverges. Bounded factors never change the verdict; the frontier behavior decides.

This is Unit 10's training ground, explicitly: series convergence runs on the same comparison logic (direct comparison, limit comparison), the same p-criterion, and the integral test literally converts series questions INTO this chapter's questions. Students solid on improper integrals find half of Unit 10 pre-learned; the investment pays forward at the course's highest-stakes unit.

The unit closes here, fully equipped: accumulation defined (ch 1), approximated (ch 2), welded to derivatives (ch 3-4), and computed by a four-technique kit (ch 5-7) that now reaches infinite domains (ch 8). Unit 7 immediately spends the equipment on differential equations — where antiderivatives become predictions and the logistic equation cashes the partial-fractions check this unit wrote.
key_terms: Under a convergent roof: converges; over a divergent floor: diverges
The integrand's behavior at ∞ (or the singularity) decides; bounded factors don't
Same logic, same p-criterion: the integral test makes the connection literal
boxes: ap_alert

'Determine whether the integral converges' does NOT always mean 'evaluate it' — comparison to a p-integral earns full credit when the question asks only for the verdict with justification. Read the ask; evaluation is sometimes the slow road to the same points.

mcq.question: ∫₁^∞ dx/x³ =
mcq.explanation: lim b→∞ [-1/(2x²)]₁ᵇ = 0 + 1/2. (p = 3 > 1: convergent, value 1/(p-1) = 1/2.)

mcq.question: Which integral diverges?
mcq.explanation: p = 1/2 < 1: divergent by the p-test. The others: p = 1.001 > 1 ✓, exponential ✓, p = 2 ✓.

mcq.question: ∫₀¹ dx/√x =
mcq.explanation: Endpoint singularity at 0: lim a→0⁺ [2√x]ₐ¹ = 2 - 0 = 2. (p = 1/2 < 1 at the spike: convergent.)

mcq.question: The evaluation ∫₋₁¹ dx/x² = [-1/x]₋₁¹ = -2 is wrong because

choices.A: the integrand has an asymptote at x = 0 inside the interval, so FTC2 never applied

mcq.explanation: 1/x² is discontinuous at 0 ∈ (-1, 1): the integral must split into two improper pieces, each divergent — the integral diverges. (A negative result for a positive integrand was the alarm.)

mcq.question: Knowing 0 ≤ 1/(x⁴ + x + 7) ≤ 1/x⁴ for x ≥ 1, one may conclude ∫₁^∞ dx/(x⁴ + x + 7)

choices.A: converges, by comparison with a convergent p-integral

mcq.explanation: Trapped under ∫₁^∞ dx/x⁴ (p = 4 > 1, convergent): the smaller integral converges. The exact value isn't determined — only the verdict.

frq.question:
Evaluate each improper integral or show it diverges, using complete limit notation.
(a) ∫₂^∞ dx/(x - 1)²
(b) ∫₁^∞ dx/(2x + 3)
(c) ∫₀^∞ x e^{-x²} dx
rubric: (a) lim b→∞ [-(x-1)^{-1}]₂ᵇ = 0 + 1 = 1: converges to 1
(b) lim b→∞ (1/2)[ln|2x+3|]₁ᵇ = ∞: diverges
Limit notation present at the first step in all three
frq.model_answer: (a) ∫₂^∞ dx/(x-1)² = lim b→∞ ∫₂ᵇ (x-1)^{-2} dx = lim b→∞ [-(x-1)^{-1}]₂ᵇ = lim b→∞ (1 - 1/(b-1)) = 1. Converges to 1. (b) lim b→∞ ∫₁ᵇ dx/(2x+3) = lim b→∞ (1/2)[ln(2x+3)]₁ᵇ = lim b→∞ (1/2)(ln(2b+3) - ln 5) = ∞. Diverges. (c) With u = x², du = 2x dx: lim b→∞ ∫₀ᵇ x e^{-x²} dx = lim b→∞ [-½e^{-x²}]₀ᵇ = lim b→∞ (½ - ½e^{-b²}) = 1/2. Converges to 1/2.

frq.question:
Consider ∫₀⁴ dx/(x - 2)^{2/3}.
(a) Explain why this integral is improper despite its finite bounds.
(b) Split appropriately and evaluate both pieces.
(c) State the value of the integral, or that it diverges.
rubric: (a) The integrand blows up at x = 2, inside [0, 4] — interior singularity
(b) Split at 2: lim t→2⁻ ∫₀ᵗ + lim s→2⁺ ∫ₛ⁴, antiderivative 3(x-2)^{1/3}
(c) Both converge: total 6·2^{1/3} = 6∛2
frq.model_answer: (a) At x = 2 — inside the interval — the denominator vanishes and the integrand is unbounded: an interior singularity makes the integral improper. (b) Split at 2. Antiderivative: ∫(x-2)^{-2/3} dx = 3(x-2)^{1/3}. Left: lim t→2⁻ [3(x-2)^{1/3}]₀ᵗ = 3(0) - 3(-2)^{1/3} = 3·2^{1/3} (since (-2)^{1/3} = -2^{1/3}). Right: lim s→2⁺ [3(x-2)^{1/3}]ₛ⁴ = 3·2^{1/3} - 0 = 3·2^{1/3}. (c) Both one-sided pieces converge, so the integral converges: 3·2^{1/3} + 3·2^{1/3} = 6∛2 ≈ 7.56. (The exponent 2/3 < 1 at the spike is why convergence was possible.)

frq.question:
A pollutant enters a lake at rate R(t) = 40/(t + 1)² grams per day, for t ≥ 0.
(a) Find the total amount of pollutant that will EVER enter the lake — set up and evaluate the appropriate improper integral.
(b) Find the time T by which half of that total has entered.
(c) The cleanup agency claims 'the inflow never stops, so the total grows without bound.' Refute the claim in one sentence using the chapter's central distinction.
rubric: (a) lim b→∞ ∫₀ᵇ 40(t+1)^{-2} dt = lim [−40/(t+1)]₀ᵇ = 40 grams
(c) A perpetual inflow with sufficiently fast decay accumulates a finite total
The decay-speed (not decay-fact) distinction articulated
frq.model_answer: (a) Total = ∫₀^∞ 40/(t+1)² dt = lim b→∞ [−40/(t+1)]₀ᵇ = lim b→∞ (40 - 40/(b+1)) = 40 grams. (b) Accumulated by time T: 40 - 40/(T+1). Setting it to 20: 40/(T+1) = 20, T + 1 = 2, T = 1 day — half of all the pollutant that will ever arrive comes in the first day. (c) The claim confuses 'never stops' with 'adds up to infinity': the inflow rate decays fast enough (like 1/t², p = 2 > 1) that the endless trickle accumulates only a finite 40 grams — convergence is about decay speed, not stopping.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: ‘The population grows at a rate proportional to its size.’ That sentence IS an equation — dP/dt = kP — and equations about rates are how science actually writes its laws. This unit teaches you to read them, check them, and solve them.
learning_objectives: Translate verbal rate statements into differential equations and back
Verify proposed solutions by substitution into the differential equation
Distinguish general solutions (families) from particular solutions (one curve)
Use initial conditions to select particular solutions
Identify equilibrium solutions where the derivative is identically zero

sections.title: Equations About Rates
sections.subtitle: Reading and writing the language
sections.body:
A differential equation (DE) relates a function to its own derivatives: dy/dx = x + y, dP/dt = kP, y'' = -y. Solving one means finding the FUNCTION(s) that make the equation true — a fundamentally different task from solving for a number, and the reason the subject feels new even though every tool involved is old.

Translation is the entry skill. 'Grows at a rate proportional to its size': dP/dt = kP. 'Cools at a rate proportional to the difference between its temperature and the room's': dT/dt = -k(T - 70) (Newton's law of cooling — the minus encodes cooling toward the room). 'The rate of change of velocity is proportional to the square of speed, opposing motion': dv/dt = -kv². Each phrase maps to a derivative, a proportionality constant, and a sign chosen by physical direction.

The reverse reading matters equally: dy/dx = xy² says 'the slope of the solution curve at any point equals the product of the x-coordinate and the square of the y-coordinate.' A DE is a slope RECIPE — at every point of the plane it dictates the direction a solution passing through must head. That pointwise reading powers slope fields next chapter.

Sign conventions are graded: decay and cooling carry negative constants (or negative signs with positive k — state which), growth positive. The AP accepts either convention WHEN DECLARED; undeclared sign ambiguity in a model is where translation points die.
key_terms: An equation relating a function to its derivatives — solved by functions, not numbers
'Rate proportional to X' ⟹ derivative = k·X, sign by physical direction
A first-order DE assigns a slope to every point — the geometric meaning
boxes: ap_alert

Newton's law of cooling is the AP's favorite translation: dT/dt = -k(T - T_room) with k > 0. The rate depends on the temperature DIFFERENCE, not the temperature — writing dT/dt = -kT is the standard mistranslation and costs the modeling point.

sections.title: Verifying Solutions
sections.subtitle: Substitute and confirm both sides
sections.body:
Checking whether y = f(x) solves a DE requires no solving at all: compute the needed derivatives of f, substitute BOTH sides of the equation, and confirm identity. Does y = e^{3x} solve y' = 3y? Left side: y' = 3e^{3x}. Right side: 3y = 3e^{3x}. Equal for all x ✓ — it solves. Does y = x³ solve it? y' = 3x² versus 3y = 3x³: equal only at isolated points, not identically — no.

Verification questions are free points with a required format: compute the left side, compute the right side, state they match for all x in the domain. The AP asks 'verify that y = ... is a solution' as the opening part of DE FRQs regularly — it tests differentiation under a new costume and warms up the equation for later parts.

Families verify with the constant intact: y = Ce^{3x} solves y' = 3y for EVERY C (the C rides through both sides). Such a family is the GENERAL solution; choosing C via a known point gives a PARTICULAR solution. y(0) = 5 forces C = 5. The family-versus-member distinction organizes the whole unit: solving produces families; initial conditions pick members.

Implicit solutions verify by implicit differentiation: does x² + y² = C solve dy/dx = -x/y? Differentiate the relation: 2x + 2y y' = 0, so y' = -x/y ✓ — for every C at once. Unit 3's machinery, now certifying solution families it could not have named.
key_terms: Differentiate the candidate, substitute both sides, confirm identity for all x
The family with arbitrary constant(s): every member solves the DE
One family member, selected by an initial condition
boxes: ap_alert

Verification answers must show BOTH sides computed separately and then equated — 'y' = 3e^{3x} = 3y ✓' is the shape. Substituting the answer into itself or asserting equality without computing both sides earns nothing.

sections.title: Initial Conditions and Uniqueness
sections.subtitle: One point, one curve
sections.body:
An initial value problem (IVP) pairs a DE with a point: dy/dx = 2xy with y(0) = 4. The DE supplies the family; the point selects the member. Geometrically: through (almost) every point of the plane passes exactly one solution curve — the DE's slope recipe, integrated forward and backward from the anchor.

The constant-pinning workflow extends Unit 6's IVPs: find the general solution (by methods to come), substitute the initial point, solve for C, write the finished function. The exam's wrinkle: pin C at the RIGHT STAGE. When the general solution involves logs or exponentials of both sides, pinning C before exponentiating is usually cleaner — and chapter 4 makes this concrete.

Domain restrictions ride with particular solutions: y = 1/(1 - x) may solve y' = y² with y(0) = 1, but only on (-∞, 1) — the branch through the initial point, ending where the solution blows up. The AP asks for solution domains on occasion, and the rule is: the largest interval CONTAINING the initial point on which the solution is defined and differentiable. The other branch, however algebraically identical, is a different solution.

Equilibrium solutions are the constant members: values where the DE's right side vanishes identically. For dP/dt = 0.2P(10 - P): P = 0 and P = 10 are equilibria — start there and the system never moves. Equilibria organize the qualitative picture (solutions between 0 and 10 grow toward 10; above 10, decay toward it) and headline the logistic analysis two chapters ahead.
key_terms: DE + anchor point: the family narrowed to one curve
The largest interval around the initial point where the solution lives
Constant solutions where the rate is identically zero — the system at rest
boxes: ap_alert

'Find all values of P for which the population is not changing' means solve dP/dt = 0 — the equilibria. It is an algebra question hiding in a calculus unit, asked nearly every time a logistic or cooling model appears.

sections.title: Models Worth Knowing
sections.subtitle: The unit's recurring cast
sections.body:
Exponential growth/decay — dy/dt = ky: the rate is proportional to the amount. Money compounding continuously, radioactive decay, unchecked populations. Solution family (chapter 5 derives it): y = Ce^{kt}. The fingerprint: relative rate y'/y is CONSTANT.

Newton's cooling — dT/dt = -k(T - T_env): the rate is proportional to the gap from the environment. Coffee cooling, bodies in forensics, thermostats. Solutions decay exponentially TOWARD T_env rather than toward zero — a shifted exponential, with the equilibrium at room temperature.

Logistic growth — dP/dt = kP(1 - P/L): growth proportional to BOTH the population and the remaining room (L is the carrying capacity). Small populations grow almost exponentially; near capacity, growth chokes; the S-curve from Unit 5's epidemic example is this equation's solution. The BC exam's signature model, fully solved in chapter 6.

Reading model behavior WITHOUT solving is the unit's quiet superpower, available now: equilibria from the algebra (set the rate to zero), increasing/decreasing regions from the rate's sign, concavity from differentiating the DE itself (d²P/dt² via the chain rule on the right side). A surprising share of DE FRQ points require no solution formula at all — just Unit 5 analysis applied to the rate equation. The solving techniques ahead are for the parts that do.
key_terms: y' = ky: constant relative rate, family Ce^{kt}
T' = -k(T - T_env): exponential approach to the environment
P' = kP(1 - P/L): growth with a ceiling — BC's signature equation
boxes: ap_alert

Behavior questions ('is P increasing? concave up?') are answerable directly from the DE — substitute the value into the rate for the first, differentiate the DE (chain rule!) for the second. Reaching for the solution formula first is the slow road; the equation already knows.

mcq.question: 'The mass decays at a rate proportional to the mass present' translates to
mcq.explanation: Rate proportional to the amount, with decay's negative sign. (C is a solution, not the equation.)

mcq.question: Which function is a solution of y' = -2y?
mcq.explanation: y' = -14e^{-2x} = -2(7e^{-2x}) = -2y ✓ — and any constant multiple works.

mcq.question: The general solution of a DE is y = Ce^{x²}. If y(0) = 3, the particular solution is
The equilibrium solutions of dP/dt = 0.5P(8 - P) are
mcq.explanation: Set the rate to zero: 0.5P(8 - P) = 0 at P = 0, 8 — the constant solutions.

mcq.question: For dT/dt = -0.3(T - 20) with T(0) = 80, the temperature T is
mcq.explanation: At T = 80 the rate is -18 < 0: cooling. The rate vanishes at T = 20 — the environmental equilibrium the solution approaches.

frq.question:
Consider the differential equation dy/dx = 3y.
(a) Verify that y = Ce^{3x} is a solution for every constant C.
(b) Find the particular solution with y(0) = 5.
(c) Verify that y = 0 is also a solution, and explain its relationship to the family in (a).
rubric: (a) y' = 3Ce^{3x} and 3y = 3Ce^{3x}: equal for all x, any C
(b) 5 = Ce⁰ = C: y = 5e^{3x}
Relationship: the equilibrium, also the family member with C = 0
frq.model_answer: (a) Left side: y' = 3Ce^{3x}. Right side: 3y = 3Ce^{3x}. The two sides agree identically for every x and every C — the whole family solves the equation. (b) y(0) = C = 5: y = 5e^{3x}. (c) For y = 0: y' = 0 and 3y = 0 ✓. It is the equilibrium solution — the system at rest — and it belongs to the family as the C = 0 member, so the general solution y = Ce^{3x} already contains it.

frq.question:
A cup of coffee at 90°C sits in a 20°C room. Its temperature obeys dT/dt = -k(T - 20) for some k > 0, t in minutes.
(a) What does the model say about the SIGN of dT/dt while T > 20, and what does that mean physically?
(b) Without solving, find lim t→∞ T(t) and justify from the equation.
(c) Differentiate the DE to show d²T/dt² = k²(T - 20), and conclude the cooling curve is concave up while T > 20.
rubric: (a) T > 20 makes -(T - 20) < 0: dT/dt < 0, the coffee cools
(b) The rate vanishes only at T = 20 (equilibrium); cooling continues while above it: T → 20
(c) d²T/dt² = -k·dT/dt = -k·(-k(T - 20)) = k²(T - 20) > 0 for T > 20
Concavity conclusion: cooling fast at first, flattening toward the room temperature
frq.model_answer: (a) While T > 20, T - 20 > 0, so dT/dt = -k(T - 20) < 0: the temperature falls — hot coffee cools, as it must. (b) The only equilibrium is T = 20. The solution decreases while above 20 and its rate shrinks as the gap closes, so T(t) → 20 as t → ∞ — the coffee approaches room temperature without crossing it. (c) Differentiating both sides in t: d²T/dt² = -k(dT/dt) = -k(-k(T - 20)) = k²(T - 20). While T > 20 this is positive: the graph is concave up — steep cooling initially, leveling off as the cup nears the room's temperature, the familiar cooling-curve shape.

frq.question:
Let y = 1/(1 - x).
(a) Verify that y solves the differential equation dy/dx = y² with y(0) = 1.
(b) State the domain of this particular solution and explain why it stops where it does.
(c) The function z = 1/(1 - x) ALSO describes a curve for x > 1. Explain why that branch is NOT the solution to this IVP.
rubric: (b) Domain (-∞, 1): the branch through x = 0, ending at the vertical asymptote x = 1
(c) The x > 1 branch does not contain the initial point
A solution must live on one interval containing the anchor; disconnected branches are different solutions
frq.model_answer: (a) y' = d/dx (1 - x)^{-1} = (1 - x)^{-2} = [1/(1 - x)]² = y² ✓, and y(0) = 1/(1 - 0) = 1 ✓. (b) The solution's domain is (-∞, 1) — the largest interval containing the initial point x = 0 on which the formula is defined. The solution blows up at the vertical asymptote x = 1 (the curve escapes to infinity in finite x) and cannot be continued past it. (c) A solution to an IVP is a differentiable function on an INTERVAL through the initial point. The x > 1 branch never touches (0, 1) — it is a separate solution of the same DE (anchored by different conditions), not part of this one. Algebraic formulas can describe several solutions at once; the initial condition picks a single connected branch.

subject: AP Calculus BC
chapter_title: Slope Fields — Seeing Solutions Before Solving
hook: Draw a tiny dash at every point showing the slope the equation demands there, and solution curves appear like iron filings around a magnet. Slope fields let you SEE every solution at once — including the ones no formula can express.
learning_objectives: Construct slope field segments at given points from a differential equation
Match differential equations to slope fields by structural features
Sketch particular solutions through given points by following the field
Read equilibria, increasing/decreasing regions, and concavity from a field
Determine where slopes are zero, undefined, or constant along lines

sections.title: Building the Field
sections.subtitle: A dash at every point
sections.body:
A slope field (direction field) plots, at each grid point (x, y), a short segment with slope dy/dx as the DE dictates there. For dy/dx = x - y at the point (2, 1): slope 1 — a 45° dash. At (0, 2): slope -2 — steep downhill. The field is the DE made visible: every dash is one evaluation of the right-hand side.

Construction questions on the AP are exactly that mechanical: 'sketch the solution segments at the twelve indicated points' means twelve evaluations and twelve dashes with reasonable slopes (zero flat, ±1 at 45°, steeper distinguished from shallower). Precision to the degree is not graded; getting zero, sign, and steep-versus-shallow right is.

Efficiency comes from level curves of slope — ISOCLINES: the set where dy/dx = c. For dy/dx = x - y, slopes are 0 exactly on the line y = x, slopes are 1 on y = x - 1 — whole diagonals of parallel dashes at once. Spotting where slopes vanish (the nullcline) organizes the entire field in one stroke and answers 'where are the dashes horizontal?' instantly.

Dependence structure shapes the field's symmetry: if the DE involves ONLY x (dy/dx = 2x), every vertical line carries identical dashes — the field is column-uniform. Only y (dy/dx = y - 3): row-uniform. Both variables: the general case. This observation is the master key to the matching genre next.
key_terms: A dash of slope f(x, y) at each grid point — the DE drawn
Where the slope equals c / equals 0: whole curves of parallel dashes
x-only DEs repeat down columns; y-only DEs repeat across rows
boxes: ap_alert

When drawing field segments, three gradations are graded: horizontal where the slope is 0, 45-degree-ish where it is ±1, visibly steeper beyond. Dashes all drawn at the same tilt — the rushed student's field — loses the construction points wholesale.

sections.title: The Matching Genre
sections.subtitle: Which equation made this field?
sections.body:
Given a field and four candidate DEs, structural tests eliminate fast. Test 1 — uniformity: columns identical ⟹ the DE has no y; rows identical ⟹ no x. Test 2 — the zero set: find the horizontal dashes; their locations must satisfy RHS = 0 (horizontal along y = x? the equation vanishes there: consistent with dy/dx = x - y, not with dy/dx = x + y). Test 3 — a single point probe: evaluate each surviving candidate at one easy point with a distinctive dash and compare signs/steepness.

The three tests in that order settle nearly every matching question in under a minute, and each test is a one-line justification if the format demands work. Sign patterns by quadrant — 'slopes positive in quadrants I and III, negative in II and IV' suggests dy/dx = xy — extend test 3 across regions for the trickier sets.

The reverse genre — given the DE, pick the field — runs the same tests generatively: predict the uniformity, predict the nullcline, predict one quadrant's signs, then find the field exhibiting all three. Predict-then-match beats staring; the structure does the work.

Distractor fields are built by sign flips (the field of -f), variable swaps (the field of f(y, x)), and nullcline shifts. The three tests catch all three manufacturing methods — which is why they are the tests.
key_terms: Uniformity, zero set, point probe — in that order
Products like xy alternate signs by quadrant; sums change along lines
Generate the features from the DE, then find the field showing them
boxes: ap_alert

The nullcline test is the highest-yield single check: locate the horizontal dashes, set each candidate's right side to zero, and keep only candidates whose zero set passes through those dashes. One test typically eliminates three of four choices.

sections.title: Threading Solutions
sections.subtitle: Curves that follow the dashes
sections.body:
A solution curve through a point P threads the field: starting at P, it proceeds tangent to every dash it meets — the dashes are the curve's own tangent segments, prescribed in advance. Sketching one is a hand-eye exercise: from P, follow the local slope a short way, reassess, continue; backward from P the same. The result should never CROSS dashes at an angle — crossing means the sketch disobeyed the equation somewhere.

Quality criteria the readers apply: the curve passes through the required point; its slope at that point matches the local dash; it respects equilibria (never crossing a horizontal-dash line that represents an equilibrium solution — solutions cannot cross each other, in particular not the constant ones); and its end behavior follows the field's flow (flattening toward equilibria, steepening where dashes steepen).

The no-crossing principle has teeth: for dP/dt = P(10 - P), a solution starting at P = 3 stays trapped in the band 0 < P < 10 forever — the equilibria at 0 and 10 are walls. Threading respects the walls: the curve rises from 3, inflects, and flattens toward 10 without touching it. The trapped-between-equilibria reading answers limit questions ('lim t→∞ P = 10') without any formula.

Multiple threads from different anchors reveal the family: sketching solutions through three stacked points shows the family's structure — for x-only DEs the members are exact vertical translates of one another, and in general they are non-crossing curves filling the plane. The field plus threading IS the general solution, drawn instead of derived.
key_terms: Following the dashes tangentially from the anchor point, both directions
Solution curves never cross each other — equilibria are impassable walls
Between equilibria, solutions stay forever: limits read off the field
boxes: ap_alert

Sketched solutions are graded on three visible behaviors: through the point, tangent to the local dashes, and asymptotic to (never crossing) equilibrium lines. A sketch that touches the equilibrium loses the point — approach, don't arrive.

sections.title: Reading Without Solving
sections.subtitle: Qualitative analysis from the picture
sections.body:
Fields answer behavior questions formula-free. Where is the solution through (1, 2) increasing? Wherever the local slopes are positive along its path — read the dash signs. Where is it concave up? Where the dashes STEEPEN in the direction of travel (slopes increasing along the curve) — or, rigorously, differentiate the DE: for dy/dx = x - y, y'' = 1 - y' = 1 - (x - y), and the sign analysis runs on the formula. Field for intuition, implicit differentiation of the DE for certification.

The d²y/dx² computation deserves its own drill since BC asks it directly: differentiate the right side with respect to x, REMEMBERING y is a function of x (chain rule fees on every y). dy/dx = xy: y'' = y + xy' = y + x(xy) = y + x²y = y(1 + x²). Concavity of solutions now reads from y's sign alone — solutions above the x-axis are concave up everywhere. One differentiation, global conclusions.
